It is well defined by the proved chart invariance and finite-union rule, and the maximum exists because the possible dimensions lie in this finite set. Combining (N6)–(N7), every compact parametrization supplied above can be replaced by a finite union of compact analytic sources of dimension at most DD, with exactly the same image. Multiplying a source of dimension d<Dd<D by the unused compact factor TD−dT^{D-d} makes its dimension exactly DD, preserves its image and preserves compactness. Alternatively apply (N6) with R=DR=D directly. These are the dimension-controlled compact sources needed for the locally finite proper assembly. The empty set uses the empty manifold, without assigning it a negative manifold dimension.

Example for the mechanism. On T2T^2, take F=u1=cos⁡θ1F=u_1=\cos\theta_1 and h=u2=cos⁡θ2h=u_2=\cos\theta_2. Then r=1r=1, A=diag⁡(−v1,−v2)A=\operatorname{diag}(-v_1,-v_2), and g=v12v22g=v_1^2v_2^2. Its zero set is the union of four coordinate circles, two given by v1=0v_1=0 and two by v2=0v_2=0. On every fibre of FF, the minimum of hh occurs on the circle (u2,v2)=(−1,0)(u_2,v_2)=(-1,0), which still maps onto the whole interval [−1,1][-1,1]. The circles v1=0v_1=0 retain the lower-rank fibres over the endpoints. This explicit example explains the equality of images; the general proof uses the full zero set and its compact monomial charts.

A locally finite assembly with a fixed source dimension

Proper uniformization. Let SS be a nonempty closed subanalytic subset of a finite-dimensional real analytic manifold XX, Hausdorff and countable at infinity. Let DD be its finite-cell dimension. There is a Hausdorff, second-countable real analytic manifold YY, of pure dimension DD, and a proper analytic map

F:Y⟶X,F(Y)=S.(N8) F:Y\longrightarrow X,\qquad F(Y)=S. \qquad\text{(N8)}

If SS is compact, YY can be compact. The empty set is represented by the empty manifold. Properness is relative to the stated ambient manifold XX.

Proof. The elementary locally finite compact chart construction, (F2)–(F4), gives a countable family of closed coordinate boxes QiQ_i, each contained in an analytic coordinate neighborhood ViV_i, with locally finite family (Qi)(Q_i) and with interiors covering XX. The boxes can be chosen subordinate to the witness neighborhoods used in the projection definition of SS. This construction uses only an exhaustion by nested compact sets and finite covers of its compact bands. It does not use uniformization or an analytic partition of unity.

Since SS is closed in XX, each Si=S∩QiS_i=S\cap Q_i is compact and subanalytic. The compact construction above represents SiS_i as a finite union of analytic images of tori. Every such image lies in SiS_i, hence entirely in the target chart ViV_i. Apply the preceding dimension-reduction lemma in that chart. It produces finitely many maps

fij:Teij⟶X,eij≤D,⋃jfij(Teij)=Si,fij(Teij)⊂Qi.(N9) f_{ij}:T^{e_{ij}}\longrightarrow X,\qquad e_{ij}\le D,\qquad \bigcup_j f_{ij}(T^{e_{ij}})=S_i, \quad f_{ij}(T^{e_{ij}})\subset Q_i. \qquad\text{(N9)}

An empty SiS_i contributes no maps. For eij<De_{ij}<D, add D−eijD-e_{ij} unused circle factors and let fijf_{ij} ignore them. This preserves its analyticity, compactness and image. Define YY as the disjoint union of these copies of TDT^D, and define FF componentwise by the corresponding maps.

There are countably many components, each a Hausdorff second-countable analytic DD-manifold. Their disjoint union is Hausdorff and second countable: unite one countable basis from each component. It has the same finite dimension DD everywhere. Componentwise charts and transition maps make FF analytic. The cover by the interiors of QiQ_i and (N9) prove F(Y)=SF(Y)=S.

To check properness, let K⊂XK\subset X be compact. Local finiteness and a finite subcover of KK show that only finitely many QiQ_i meet KK. Thus F−1(K)F^{-1}(K) lies in finitely many of the compact source tori. It is closed there, because KK is closed in the Hausdorff space XX and FF is continuous. Consequently F−1(K)F^{-1}(K) is compact. This proves properness without requiring the images of different source components to be disjoint.

When SS is compact, finitely many of the chosen interior boxes cover it. Using just those boxes and their finitely many tori gives a compact YY, and the same image equality. The dimension-zero case uses T0T^0, a point, and the same locally finite argument. ▫\square

The dimension in (N8) also equals the supremum of the dimensions of intrinsic analytic regular points, as used in item 2. Here only that numerical equality is needed; it does not assert subanalyticity of the entire regular locus. To prove it, choose a bounded open coordinate box UU, with closure inside a witness neighborhood, such that dim⁡(S∩U)=D\dim(S\cap U)=D. Take a finite analytic cell decomposition of S∩US\cap U containing a cell CC of dimension DD. Every point of this trace lies in the open set UU, so its cells describe SS near that point. For every other cell C′C', its intersection with CC is empty, and

C∩C′¯⊂C′¯\C′,dim⁡(C′¯\C′)<dim⁡C′≤D.(N10) C\cap\overline{C'}\subset\overline{C'}\setminus C', \qquad \dim(\overline{C'}\setminus C')<\dim C'\le D. \qquad\text{(N10)}

The finite-cell dimension and strict-frontier theorems imply that these finitely many intersections cannot cover CC. Choose p∈Cp\in C outside every C′¯\overline{C'}. A small ambient neighborhood meets no other cell. As an embedded analytic submanifold, CC is closed in a sufficiently small neighborhood of pp, and there S=CS=C. Thus pp is an intrinsic regular point of dimension DD. Conversely, a regular dd-dimensional manifold piece contained in SS has d≤Dd\le D by manifold dimension and monotonicity. This gives the claimed numerical equality. The analytic-descent proof below establishes definability of the entire intrinsic regular locus.

A compact fibre meets the minimizing circle

Figure. Write each circle as (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(\cos\theta,\sin\theta) or (cos⁡ϕ,sin⁡ϕ)(\cos\phi,\sin\phi). For f(θ,ϕ)=cos⁡θf(\theta,\phi)=\cos\theta and h(θ,ϕ)=cos⁡ϕh(\theta,\phi)=\cos\phi, the squared determinant is g=sin⁡2θsin⁡2ϕg=\sin^2\theta\sin^2\phi. Exercises on dimension control and properness

Exercise N1 (intermediate: retaining singular fibres). In the displayed torus model, compute the set ZZ, verify that it meets the fibres over 11 and −1-1, and exhibit a one-dimensional compact analytic source with the same image as the original two-dimensional torus.

Solution. The matrix of d(f,h)d(f,h) in the angular frame is diagonal with entries −sin⁡θ-\sin\theta and −sin⁡ϕ-\sin\phi. Hence ZZ is the union of the circles θ=0\theta=0, θ=π\theta=\pi, ϕ=0\phi=0, and ϕ=π\phi=\pi, with angles interpreted modulo 2π2\pi. The endpoint fibres are the entire first two circles, so they are retained, not discarded as exceptional. The circle ϕ=π\phi=\pi maps by θ↦cos⁡θ\theta\mapsto\cos\theta onto [−1,1][-1,1]. It is a compact one-dimensional analytic source with the full image. An interior fibre has two points on this selected circle; an endpoint fibre has one. No injectivity or preservation of the original fibres is part of uniformization.

Exercise N2 (intermediate: componentwise properness is insufficient). Let YY be a countable disjoint union of points and map every point to 0∈ℝ0\in\mathbb R. Explain why every component map is proper, but the combined map is not. Also distinguish properness of the identity of (0,1)(0,1) from properness of its inclusion into ℝ\mathbb R.

Solution. Each point is compact, so its map is proper. The inverse image of the compact set {0}\{0\} under the combined map is the infinite discrete space YY; its cover by singleton open sets has no finite subcover. The image supports are not a locally finite family, which is exactly the hypothesis used in the proof of (N8). The identity of (0,1)(0,1) is proper because inverse images of compact subsets are those same subsets. Its inclusion into ℝ\mathbb R is not proper: the inverse image of [0,1][0,1] is all of (0,1)(0,1), which is not compact. Therefore the ambient target in a proper uniformization statement must be retained.

Detecting the entire analytic regular locus

A cell partition supplies many analytic manifold points. Recognizing every such point, including points crossed by an unnecessary cell boundary, requires a test independent of the partition. We will use analyticity of squared distance to a closed set, after proving that a continuous subanalytic function has a subanalytic analyticity locus.

The graphic-point mechanism comes from Malgrange, as used by Bierstone and Milman in Semianalytic and subanalytic sets, §7, printed pp. 37–41, especially Proposition 7.4 and Theorems 7.5–7.10. The proof below expands the local convergence and compact descent arguments. It uses compact uniformization and the compact rank reduction (N6); the locally finite noncompact uniformization assembly and a finite-smoothness version of Tamm’s theorem are not inputs.

The complex analytic providers are the proved contour preparation and division theorem, unique factorization of holomorphic germs, and finite branches with connected dense smooth cores. These concern complex analytic sets and do not assume the real subanalytic regular-locus statement being proved.

Convergence at a critical source point

First, if a,ba,b are convergent complex power series, b≠0b\ne0, and a=bHa=bH for a formal series HH, then HH converges. Make bb regular in one variable and write b=uPb=uP, with PP distinguished. Divide a/ua/u analytically by PP. Uniqueness of formal division by the same distinguished polynomial makes the analytic remainder zero and identifies the analytic quotient with HH. Formal division follows coefficient by coefficient in the other variables: modulo their successive powers, division by the leading power of the distinguished variable determines quotient and remainder.

Lemma. Let ψ:(ℂm,0)→(ℂn,0)\psi:(\mathbb C^m,0)\to(\mathbb C^n,0) be holomorphic of generic rank nn. If G∈ℂ[[y]]G\in\mathbb C[[y]] and f=G∘ψf=G\circ\psi converges, then GG converges.

Proof. The case n=0n=0 is constant and immediate. Choose a nonzero nn-rowed Jacobian minor δ\delta, after reordering source coordinates. On δ≠0\delta\ne0, differentiation with respect to the first coordinates in (ψ1,…,ψn,xn+1,…,xm)(\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_n,x_{n+1},\ldots,x_m) has the form Dj=δ−1∑ℓ=1nAjℓ(x)∂xℓ,Djψi=δij, D_j=\delta^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^n A_{j\ell}(x)\partial_{x_\ell}, \qquad D_j\psi_i=\delta_{ij}, with holomorphic cofactors AjℓA_{j\ell}. Set Fβ=DβfF_\beta=D^\beta f. Its numerator is holomorphic on one fixed sufficiently small source neighborhood and its denominator is a power of δ\delta. Formal differentiation gives Fβ=(∂βG)∘ψ∈ℂ[[x]],Fβ(0)=∂βG(0). F_\beta=(\partial^\beta G)\circ\psi\in\mathbb C[[x]], \qquad F_\beta(0)=\partial^\beta G(0). Here the equality is first in the fraction field of formal series; its right side lies in the formal series ring. The divisibility observation makes every FβF_\beta holomorphic as a germ at zero.

Moreover df=∑jFejdψjdf=\sum_jF_{e_j}\,d\psi_j as a germ. The meromorphic identity extends to the fixed connected source neighborhood. Thus, wherever δ≠0\delta\ne0, ff is independent of the unused local coordinates, and is a holomorphic function of ψ\psi alone. The DjD_j commute there, so the derivative order used to define FβF_\beta is immaterial.

We now obtain one neighborhood for all FβF_\beta. Make an additional linear source change so δ\delta is regular in a variable zz, and prepare δ(z,x′)=u(z,x′)P(z,x′). \delta(z,x')=u(z,x')P(z,x'). The already defined meromorphic operators are simply transported under this change. Retain the original complementary functions ℓ=(xn+1,…,xm)\ell=(x_{n+1},\ldots,x_m) as fixed linear functions in the new coordinates; they are not replaced by arbitrary new coordinate functions. The map (ψ,ℓ)(\psi,\ell) remains a local coordinate system wherever δ≠0\delta\ne0. Choose a circle |z|=r|z|=r and a connected smaller x′x'-polydisc such that P≠0P\ne0 on the circle and all roots of P(⋅,x′)P(\,\cdot\,,x') lie strictly inside it. The original holomorphic functions and the unit uu are defined on a neighborhood of the closed cylinder.

For every β\beta, write Fβ=hβ/PqβF_\beta=h_\beta/P^{q_\beta}, with hβh_\beta holomorphic on that fixed neighborhood. The contour division formula divides hβh_\beta by the monic polynomial PqβP^{q_\beta} on the same cylinder, producing a polynomial remainder whose coefficients are holomorphic throughout the fixed x′x'-polydisc. At the origin this remainder vanishes as a germ: FβF_\beta was holomorphic there, so uniqueness of Weierstrass division applies. The coefficient identity theorem makes it zero on the whole connected x′x'-polydisc. Consequently every FβF_\beta is holomorphic on the common interior cylinder. No bound on qβq_\beta is required; the same circle avoids the zeros of all denominators.

On the compact circle K={(z,0):|z|=r}K=\{(z,0):|z|=r\}, use the local inverse of (ψ,ℓ)(\psi,\ell) to form Hi(x,t)=f((ψ,ℓ)−1(ψ(x)+t,ℓ(x))). H_i(x,t)=f\bigl((\psi,\ell)^{-1}(\psi(x)+t,\ell(x))\bigr). At each point of KK, this is holomorphic on a product of a source neighborhood and a positive target polydisc. Shrink both so it is bounded on their closures. The source neighborhoods have a finite subcover of KK. Taking the largest of their bounds and the smallest target radius gives constants C,ρ>0C,\rho>0 such that Cauchy’s estimate yields |Fβ(x)|=|∂tβHi(x,0)|≤Cβ!ρ−|β|(x∈K) |F_\beta(x)|=|\partial_t^\beta H_i(x,0)| \le C\,\beta!\,\rho^{-|\beta|} \qquad(x\in K) for every multi-index. The equality uses the retained complementary functions, so these are exactly the transported operators DjD_j. No gluing of the functions HiH_i is needed for the estimate.

The common-cylinder holomorphic extension and Cauchy’s formula in zz, with x′=0x'=0, give |∂βG(0)|=|Fβ(0)|≤Cβ!ρ−|β|. |\partial^\beta G(0)|=|F_\beta(0)| \le C\,\beta!\,\rho^{-|\beta|}. Thus the coefficients of G=∑βcβyβG=\sum_\beta c_\beta y^\beta satisfy |cβ|≤Cρ−|β||c_\beta|\le C\rho^{-|\beta|}. The product of the nn geometric series proves absolute convergence when every |yj|<ρ|y_j|<\rho. This proves convergence at the original, possibly critical, source point. ▫\square

The local obstruction to an analytic graph

Let ϕ:M→N\phi:M\to N and f:M→ℝf:M\to\mathbb R be analytic, with dim⁡N=n\dim N=n. Assume that ϕ\phi has generic rank nn on every component of MM, and that rank⁡d(ϕ,f)=nwhere rank⁡dϕ=n.(IR1) \operatorname{rank}d(\phi,f)=n \quad\text{where }\operatorname{rank}d\phi=n. \qquad\text{(IR1)} A point a∈Ma\in M is graphic if an analytic germ hh at ϕ(a)\phi(a) satisfies fa=h∘ϕaf_a=h\circ\phi_a. Such an hh is unique. Regular points of ϕ\phi occur arbitrarily near aa, and their images contain open target sets. Equality of two pullbacks therefore forces equality of the two target germs by the analytic identity theorem.

Condition (IR1) is necessary: ϕ(x,z)=x\phi(x,z)=x, f(x,z)=zf(x,z)=z has no graphic points, although ϕ\phi has full rank. For a parametrization of a function’s graph, (IR1) is automatic, since ff is constant on each local fibre at a submersion point.

One-point obstruction lemma. The non-graphic set EE is closed real analytic and lies in the critical set of ϕ\phi.

Proof. Complexify small real coordinate neighborhoods. The differential identities in (IR1) extend holomorphically. Choose a nonzero Jacobian minor δ\delta, and form the meromorphic functions Fβ=DβfF_\beta=D^\beta f used in the convergence lemma. Off δ=0\delta=0, condition (IR1) makes ff locally a function of ϕ\phi, and the FβF_\beta are its descended derivatives. Their denominators are powers of δ\delta.

Suppose all FβF_\beta are holomorphic at aa. Define Ga(t)=∑βFβ(a)β!tβ.(IR2) G_a(t)=\sum_\beta\frac{F_\beta(a)}{\beta!}t^\beta . \qquad\text{(IR2)} For every kk, the Taylor-composition identities through degree kk hold at regular points. They are holomorphic identities involving only finitely many FβF_\beta, so extend to aa. Hence f̂a=Ga(ϕ̂a−ϕ(a)). \widehat f_a=G_a(\widehat\phi_a-\phi(a)). The convergence lemma makes GaG_a convergent, so aa is graphic. Conversely, a graphic germ hh gives Fβ=(∂βh)∘ϕF_\beta=(\partial^\beta h)\circ\phi, so every FβF_\beta is holomorphic. Thus EE is exactly the union of their pole loci.

This infinite union is analytic for a specific reason. Shrink to a fixed complex neighborhood where {δ=0}\{\delta=0\} has finitely many irreducible hypersurface components. Each meromorphic function with denominator a power of δ\delta has pole locus equal to a union of some of these components. Local unique factorization tests which denominator factors cancel. On the connected dense smooth core of an irreducible component, the identity theorem propagates such cancellation along the component; local factorization then extends it at its remaining points. A genuine uncancelled factor instead gives a pole along the entire component, because the holomorphic locus is open. Local unique factorization also excludes a pole supported only in smaller codimension. Therefore the union of all the pole loci is a union of a subset of the same finite list of components, hence analytic.

Conjugation preserves the construction. Denote its complex analytic pole set by EℂE^{\mathbb C}. At a real point any complex descended germ equals its conjugate, since their pullbacks agree and descent is unique. Thus the real non-graphic set is exactly E=Eℂ∩ME=E^{\mathbb C}\cap M. Retain the constructed complex set, which can be larger than a minimal complexification of this real trace. Using any nonzero minor shows that every regular point of ϕ\phi is graphic. These local sets agree because their defining property is intrinsic. ▫\square

Comparing two points of a fibre

The fibre product R=M×NM={(a,b):ϕ(a)=ϕ(b)}(IR3) R=M\times_NM=\{(a,b):\phi(a)=\phi(b)\} \qquad\text{(IR3)} is analytic. A pair is graphic if one germ hh works at both points. Write E2E_2 for the pairs that are not graphic.

Two-point obstruction lemma. The subset E2E_2 is closed analytic.

Proof. Work directly on complexifications of the two source charts and their common target chart, and use the complex pole sets EℂE^{\mathbb C} constructed in the preceding proof. Write RℂR^{\mathbb C} for the resulting holomorphic fibre product. A complex graphic pair stays graphic on a neighborhood, using the same representative hh, so its non-graphic set E2ℂE_2^{\mathbb C} is closed. Put Bℂ=Rℂ∩((Eℂ×Mℂ)∪(Mℂ×Eℂ)), B^{\mathbb C}=R^{\mathbb C}\cap \bigl((E^{\mathbb C}\times M^{\mathbb C}) \cup(M^{\mathbb C}\times E^{\mathbb C})\bigr), using the appropriate source chart in each factor. This analytic set is contained in E2ℂE_2^{\mathbb C}. In particular, BℂB^{\mathbb C} is formed from the actual complex pole loci, not from an arbitrary complexification of their possibly smaller real traces.

On Rℂ\BℂR^{\mathbb C}\setminus B^{\mathbb C}, agreement of the two descended germs is locally constant. Near a pair, represent the two germs by holomorphic functions h1,h2h_1,h_2 on one connected target ball. Either they agree identically, or their germs agree nowhere on that ball: germ equality would imply equality on an open set and then everywhere. Uniqueness of descent identifies these with the germs at all nearby pairs.

Take finite irreducible branch representatives RiR_i of RℂR^{\mathbb C} at the pair. A branch contained in BℂB^{\mathbb C} is wholly bad. On every other branch, take a connected dense smooth core and delete BℂB^{\mathbb C}. The complex branch and analytic-deletion results make this a connected dense set, on which the locally constant condition is either always good or always bad. In the bad case, closedness puts the whole branch in E2ℂE_2^{\mathbb C}. In the good case, every point of the branch outside BℂB^{\mathbb C} is good, since its neighborhood meets the dense good core and the condition is locally constant there. Hence, after a common shrinking, E2ℂ=Bℂ∪⋃bad branches iRi.(IR4) E_2^{\mathbb C}=B^{\mathbb C}\ \cup\!\!\bigcup_{\text{bad branches }i}R_i . \qquad\text{(IR4)} This is analytic. Connected cores are retained on their original larger representatives until the final shrinking; connectedness of an arbitrary smaller branch intersection is not assumed. Conjugation and uniqueness identify the real trace with E2E_2, proving the claim. ▫\square

Analyticity of a continuous subanalytic function

Analytic-locus theorem. If g:V→ℝg:V\to\mathbb R is continuous and subanalytic on an open subset of an analytic manifold, then 𝒜(g)={x∈V:g is analytic on a neighborhood of x}(IR5) \mathcal A(g)=\{x\in V:g\text{ is analytic on a neighborhood of }x\} \qquad\text{(IR5)} is open and subanalytic.

Proof. Openness is part of the definition. In a coordinate chart, choose a closed box QQ whose interior contains the point being considered and whose closure lies in VV. The graph of g|Qg|_Q is compact, closed and subanalytic. Compact uniformization gives a compact analytic manifold MM and an analytic map Φ=(ϕ,f):M⟶ℝn×ℝ,Φ(M)=graph⁡(g|Q). \Phi=(\phi,f):M\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R, \qquad \Phi(M)=\operatorname{graph}(g|_Q).

Discard components on which the generic rank of ϕ\phi is less than nn. There are finitely many components, since MM is compact. For a discarded component CC, put r=max⁡Crank⁡dϕ<nr=\max_C\operatorname{rank}d\phi<n. The compact rank reduction (N6) writes ϕ(C)\phi(C) as a finite union of analytic images of TrT^r. The image-dimension inequality (D5), applied to those compact torus maps in bounded charts, gives dim⁡ϕ(C)≤r<n\dim\phi(C)\le r<n. Thus each discarded image has empty interior. The images of the retained components form a compact, hence closed, set containing the dense complement in QQ of the discarded images. They therefore cover all of QQ. The retained map still covers the graph, has generic rank nn on every component, and f=g∘ϕf=g\circ\phi supplies (IR1).

The closed analytic set E2E_2 in the compact fibre product has compact subanalytic image under (a,b)↦ϕ(a)(a,b)\mapsto\phi(a), by the already proved proper-image calculus. We claim 𝒜(g)∩int⁡Q=int⁡Q\ϕ(E2).(IR6) \mathcal A(g)\cap\operatorname{int}Q =\operatorname{int}Q\setminus\phi(E_2). \qquad\text{(IR6)} If gg is analytic near yy, its germ works at every pair above yy.

Conversely, suppose there is no bad pair above yy. Diagonal pairs show that each individual point of the fibre is graphic. Fix a0a_0 in the fibre. Its pairs with all other points, and uniqueness of descent at a0a_0, show that every descended germ is one common germ hh. Compactness of the fibre gives finitely many source neighborhoods WiW_i covering it on which f=h∘ϕf=h\circ\phi, after choosing a common representative and shrinking its target neighborhood. The compact set M\⋃iWiM\setminus\bigcup_iW_i has closed image missing yy. A smaller target neighborhood U⊂int⁡QU\subset\operatorname{int}Q thus has ϕ−1(U)⊂⋃iWi\phi^{-1}(U)\subset\bigcup_iW_i. Every point of UU has a preimage; there g=f=hg=f=h. Hence gg is analytic near yy, proving (IR6) and subanalyticity.

The test considers every pair of points of each fibre. Neither a bound on fibre components nor a dimension bound shared with parametrizations on other target charts is needed. ▫\square

Squared distance recognizes an analytic submanifold

For a nonempty closed C⊂ℝnC\subset\mathbb R^n, put q(x)=d(x,C)2q(x)=d(x,C)^2. At a∈Ca\in C, q is analytic near a⟺C is an analytic submanifold near a.(IR7) q\text{ is analytic near }a \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\text{ is an analytic submanifold near }a. \qquad\text{(IR7)}

Proof. If CC is analytic near a=0a=0, rotate coordinates so it is the graph (u,η(u))(u,\eta(u)), with η(0)=0\eta(0)=0, Dη(0)=0D\eta(0)=0. The analytic normal-coordinate map (u,w)⟼(u,η(u))+(−Dη(u)tw,w) (u,w)\longmapsto(u,\eta(u))+(-D\eta(u)^tw,w) has invertible derivative at zero. A nearest point to xx sufficiently close to zero lies in this graph, since its distance from zero is at most 2|x|2|x|. Its displacement from xx is normal to the graph by stationarity of squared distance. The inverse-function theorem gives a unique such point π(x)\pi(x), analytic in xx. Thus q(x)=|x−π(x)|2q(x)=|x-\pi(x)|^2 is analytic.

Conversely assume qq analytic near aa. Every first derivative of qq vanishes on CC, since q≥0q\ge0 and q|C=0q|_C=0. Choose an analytic submanifold LL of smallest dimension containing the germ of CC at aa; the ambient space is one candidate. If q|L=0q|_L=0 near aa, then C=LC=L there. Otherwise choose xν∈L\Cx_\nu\in L\setminus C tending to aa, and nearest points yν∈Cy_\nu\in C. Both sequences tend to aa and eventually lie in LL. Pass to a subsequence with vν=xν−yν|xν−yν|⟶v∈TaL,|v|=1. v_\nu=\frac{x_\nu-y_\nu}{|x_\nu-y_\nu|}\longrightarrow v\in T_aL, \qquad |v|=1. The tangent assertion follows by expressing LL as a differentiable graph and estimating the difference of two graph values by its derivative near aa.

On the segment from yνy_\nu to xνx_\nu, distance to CC equals distance to yνy_\nu. One inequality uses yν∈Cy_\nu\in C; the reverse follows by the triangle inequality measured from xνx_\nu. Thus D2q(yν)[vν,vν]=2,D2q(a)[v,v]=2. D^2q(y_\nu)[v_\nu,v_\nu]=2, \qquad D^2q(a)[v,v]=2. The function x↦dqx(v)x\mapsto dq_x(v) vanishes on CC and has nonzero derivative in the tangent direction vv at aa. Its zero hypersurface cuts LL transversely, producing a smaller-dimensional analytic submanifold still containing the germ of CC. This contradiction proves (IR7). ▫\square

At a regular point of local dimension dd, the same normal coordinates give D2q(a)=2pr⁡(TaC)⟂,rank⁡D2q(a)=n−d.(IR8) D^2q(a)=2\,\operatorname{pr}_{(T_aC)^\perp}, \qquad \operatorname{rank}D^2q(a)=n-d. \qquad\text{(IR8)}

Every intrinsic regular point, in each dimension

Let SS be subanalytic in an nn-dimensional analytic manifold. Work in a relatively compact chart and close a slightly larger bounded trace of SS to get a compact subanalytic set CC; in a smaller region CC is the ambient closure of SS. The empty case is immediate.

The function q=d(⋅,C)2q=d(\,\cdot\,,C)^2 is continuous and globally subanalytic in these coordinates. Its graph is given by the minimum of polynomial squared distance over the compact definable set CC; the minimum and its equality condition are formulas with quantifiers over definable sets. Boolean and projection closure therefore give subanalyticity. The triangle inequality gives continuity. Equations (IR5)–(IR7) yield Reg⁡(C)=C∩𝒜(q). \operatorname{Reg}(C)=C\cap\mathcal A(q).

On any smaller bounded working region, bounded-chart comparison makes the subanalytic open set 𝒜(q)\mathcal A(q) definable. Its Hessian entries are subanalytic. Indeed, the graph of a derivative wherever it exists is expressed by the quantified ε,δ\varepsilon,\delta condition for the difference-quotient limit. Boolean and projection closure give definability; apply this twice on the analytic open set. Rank is expressed by finitely many minors. Hence Reg⁡d(C)=C∩𝒜(q)∩{rank⁡D2q=n−d}(IR9) \operatorname{Reg}_d(C) =C\cap\mathcal A(q)\cap\{\operatorname{rank}D^2q=n-d\} \qquad\text{(IR9)} is subanalytic for every dd.

For a set that is not closed, the exact local identity is Reg⁡d(S)=Reg⁡d(S¯)\S¯\S¯.(IR10) \operatorname{Reg}_d(S) =\operatorname{Reg}_d(\overline S) \setminus\overline{\overline S\setminus S}. \qquad\text{(IR10)} If SS agrees with a closed analytic submanifold on a neighborhood, so does its ambient closure, and missing points cannot approach the selected point. Conversely, outside the second closure in (IR10), SS and S¯\overline S agree on a neighborhood. This proves the identity. The previously proved local calculus now makes every Reg⁡d(S)\operatorname{Reg}_d(S), their finite union Reg⁡(S)\operatorname{Reg}(S), and S\Reg⁡(S)S\setminus\operatorname{Reg}(S) subanalytic. Regularity is relatively open in SS, so its complement is relatively closed.

Regular points are dense in SS. In any sufficiently small bounded open chart meeting SS, choose a finite analytic cell partition of the trace and a cell AA of maximal dimension dd. For every other cell BB, A∩B¯⊂B¯\B. A\cap\overline B\subset\overline B\setminus B. The strict frontier theorem gives dimension less than dd for this intersection, since dim⁡B≤d\dim B\le d. These finitely many intersections cannot cover AA. At a point of AA outside all the other cell closures, the entire set agrees locally with AA. An embedded analytic cell is locally closed; shrinking the neighborhood makes it a closed analytic submanifold there. This is an intrinsic regular point. Every ambient neighborhood meeting SS consequently meets Reg⁡(S)\operatorname{Reg}(S).

The same argument identifies cell dimension with the supremum of dimensions of regular germs. It produces a regular germ of maximal cell dimension, while a dd-dimensional regular germ cannot be covered by finitely many smaller-dimensional cells, by the cell-dimension volume argument. This proves all assertions of item 2, including every fixed-dimensional part. It does not identify regularity with membership in a chosen top stratum.

Exercise: separate graphic germs need not agree

Let MM be two disjoint circles u2+v2=1u^2+v^2=1, and define (ϕ+,f+)(u,v)=(u2,u2),(ϕ−,f−)(u,v)=(−u2,u2). (\phi_+,f_+)(u,v)=(u^2,u^2),\qquad (\phi_-,f_-)(u,v)=(-u^2,u^2). Their union parametrizes the compact graph of g(x)=|x|g(x)=|x|, −1≤x≤1-1\le x\le1. Show that every source point is graphic, while the target germ at zero is not analytic.

Solution. On the positive circle the descended germ is h+(x)=xh_+(x)=x; on the negative circle it is h−(x)=−xh_-(x)=-x. The identities hold even where dϕ±=0d\phi_\pm=0, so the one-point obstruction is empty. At zero a pair with one point from each circle cannot share one descended germ: uniqueness would require x=−xx=-x as germs. Thus the two-point obstruction has an image at zero. The one-sided derivatives of gg there are 11 and −1-1. Equality of fibre values alone misses this disagreement of germs.

The two maps in the exercise are analytic on their full source circles. The purple points all lie over zero; a pair from opposite circles has the same function value but no common analytic germ. This is the distinction tested by (IR3)–(IR6). Full-size diagram · Reproducible Python source.

Compatible locally finite analytic partitions

The finite analytic cell theorem, its Boolean and projection calculus, and its bounded-chart comparison give the following manifold partition. The compact chart-ball refinement is proved below in Section 2 of the cutoff construction. These are the exact inputs; no analytic regular-locus theorem or uniformization theorem is needed for this partition.

Partition theorem. Let MM be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable real analytic manifold without boundary, and let {Aa}a∈I\{A_a\}_{a\in I} be a locally finite family of locally subanalytic subsets. There is a countable locally finite partition of MM into connected locally subanalytic embedded analytic submanifolds compatible with every AaA_a: each partition member is contained in or disjoint from each AaA_a. Given finitely many analytic maps fj:M→Njf_j:M\to N_j to real analytic manifolds, the partition can also make every restriction fj|Sf_j|_S have constant rank.

Compact chart pieces and compatibility

The compact exhaustion and shell construction in the linked cutoff proof supplies a countable cover by open coordinate balls BiB_i with compact closures Li=Bi¯L_i=\overline{B_i} contained in analytic charts; the family of these closures is locally finite. For instance, use the inner balls in that construction: their closures are contained in its locally finite outer compact balls. Each ball and its closure is locally semianalytic. In its chart it has a squared-norm inequality, and outside its compact closure it is empty on a neighborhood. The exhaustion sets need not be subanalytic; only the selected balls enter the partition.

For the map assertion apply this refinement to the open cover consisting of intersections of a source chart and inverse images of target charts for the finitely many fjf_j. Thus each LiL_i lies in one source chart, and every fj(Li)f_j(L_i) lies in one selected target chart. The source and target coordinate images of these compact sets are bounded. The maps in these coordinates are analytic on a neighborhood of LiL_i.

Every compact set meets only finitely many members of a locally finite family. Indeed, cover the compact set by finitely many neighborhoods, each meeting finitely many family members; combine their finite lists. In particular LiL_i meets only finitely many LkL_k and finitely many nonempty AaA_a.

Enumerate the balls and put

Ei=Bi\⋃k<iBk.(P1) E_i=B_i\setminus\bigcup_{k<i}B_k. \qquad\text{(P1)}

These sets are disjoint and cover MM, because each point has a first containing ball. For fixed ii the earlier union is finite; its trace near LiL_i uses only the finitely many earlier closures that meet a sufficiently small neighborhood of LiL_i. To justify that neighborhood, first take a finite cover of LiL_i by neighborhoods meeting only finitely many closures, then discard the finitely many closures missing LiL_i by shrinking around that compact set. Thus EiE_i is a finite Boolean combination of locally semianalytic balls near LiL_i. The local Boolean calculus also makes every relevant Aa∩EiA_a\cap E_i locally subanalytic there.

In the chosen source coordinates, these traces are bounded and locally subanalytic at every point of their ambient closures. Their closures lie inside the compact coordinate image of LiL_i, strictly inside the source chart. Extension by the empty set therefore creates no chart-boundary obstruction. The proved bounded-chart comparison makes EiE_i and all the finitely many relevant Aa∩EiA_a\cap E_i globally subanalytic in this Euclidean space.

Apply the finite analytic cell theorem compatibly with these sets, and keep just the cells in EiE_i. Each kept cell is a connected embedded analytic submanifold. Its global subanalyticity gives local subanalyticity in the source chart, including at points of its closure; compact containment gives local emptiness outside that chart. It is therefore locally subanalytic in MM. It lies in or misses every AaA_a, including those whose trace on LiL_i is empty.

There are finitely many kept cells for each ii, and each is contained in LiL_i. A neighborhood meeting only finitely many LiL_i consequently meets only finitely many kept cells. They give a countable locally finite partition of MM. This proves the first assertion. It uses local finiteness of the compact closures; a merely countable atlas does not supply that conclusion.

Analytic coordinates on a cell

We spell out the cell coordinates needed for rank refinement. A cylindrical analytic cell CC of dimension dd has a coordinate projection q:C→Vq:C\to V which is a definable analytic diffeomorphism onto an open definable V⊂ℝdV\subset\mathbb R^d. Keep precisely its band coordinates and discard its graph coordinates.

This follows by induction through the cylindrical construction. For a graph over a cell with inverse parametrization ϕ\phi, use u↦(ϕ(u),ζ(ϕ(u)))u\mapsto(\phi(u),\zeta(\phi(u))); the old free-coordinate domain remains open. For a band over that cell, the new free domain is

{(u,t):u∈V,ζ−(ϕ(u))<t<ζ+(ϕ(u))}.(P2) \{(u,t):u\in V,\ \zeta_-(\phi(u))<t<\zeta_+(\phi(u))\}. \qquad\text{(P2)}

It is open because the endpoints are continuous, omitting the corresponding inequality for an infinite endpoint. Its inverse parametrization is (u,t)↦(ϕ(u),t)(u,t)\mapsto(\phi(u),t). These maps and their inverses are analytic. Their graphs are definable by the graph, composition and projection calculus; hence the domains are definable too. In dimension zero use the single point ℝ0\mathbb R^0. This proves the coordinate assertion, including the analytic embedding and its inverse, directly from the cell definition.

Definable derivatives and restriction ranks

Fix a kept cell C⊂EiC\subset E_i, and write ϕ:V→C\phi:V\to C for this inverse parametrization. In the chosen target coordinates the maps gj=fj∘ϕg_j=f_j\circ\phi are analytic and definable. To check the latter assertion, the coordinate graph of fjf_j over LiL_i is bounded and locally semianalytic at every point of its compact closure: its defining analytic equation is valid on a neighborhood of LiL_i, and the closed coordinate ball supplies the domain condition. The bounded-chart comparison gives a globally subanalytic graph. Restriction to CC and composition with ϕ\phi preserve definability.

For a scalar analytic definable g:V→ℝg:V\to\mathbb R, the derivative graph, with u∈Vu\in V, is described by

v=∂ℓg(u)⟺∀ϵ>0∃δ>0∀h∈ℝ,(0<|h|<δand u+heℓ∈V)⟹|g(u+heℓ)−g(u)h−v|<ϵ.(P3) \begin{aligned} v=\partial_\ell g(u) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad &\forall\epsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall h\in\mathbb R,\\ &\bigl(0<|h|<\delta\ \text{and }u+he_\ell\in V\bigr)\\ &\hspace{1em}\Longrightarrow \left|\frac{g(u+he_\ell)-g(u)}h-v\right|<\epsilon. \end{aligned} \qquad\text{(P3)}

Function values here can be written using extra real variables in the graph of gg; division by h≠0h\ne0 is a polynomial graph condition. The formula uses finitely many real quantifiers. Existential quantification is projection, and universal quantification is complement of an existentially quantified complement. Thus the established Boolean and projection calculus makes this derivative graph definable. Openness of VV supplies a nontrivial interval of allowed hh at every uu, so the limit condition specifies the derivative uniquely. Applying this to every scalar coordinate gives definable differential matrices for all gjg_j.

All rank sets are consequently definable: rank rr means that every (r+1)(r+1)-minor vanishes and, when r>0r>0, some rr-minor is nonzero. Rank zero means every matrix entry vanishes. Include all finitely many rank sets for the finitely many maps in a finite analytic cell decomposition of VV.

Every resulting dd-dimensional cell D⊂VD\subset V is open in VV. Indeed, a full-dimensional cylindrical cell has only band steps, and (P2) proves openness at every such step. Therefore ϕ(D)\phi(D) is open in CC; its tangent space is that of CC, and every fj|ϕ(D)f_j|_{\phi(D)} has the constant rank selected on DD. Retain these members as finished.

On a smaller cell DD, the old differential rank is insufficient: restricting a rank-one map to one of its level curves can give rank zero. Take the cell’s own free-coordinate parametrization ψ:W→D\psi:W\to D, and repeat the rank calculation for all gj∘ψg_j\circ\psi. These are still definable analytic maps on an open definable domain. Their images under ϕ∘ψ\phi\circ\psi are connected embedded analytic submanifolds and definable in the original source chart. Repeat the same finite refinement and finish its full-dimensional members.

An unfinished branch now has strictly smaller dimension. Induction on dd terminates: dimension zero has rank zero for every map, and each positive-dimensional step finishes its full-dimensional cells and passes only finitely many smaller cells to already established lower-dimensional cases. The final refinement of each original CC is finite. Its members remain inside LiL_i, so refining the finitely many cells for each ii preserves countability, local finiteness and compatibility with all AaA_a. This proves simultaneous constant rank on every final member. ▫\square

If MM is compact, this locally finite partition is finite by the compactness argument above. Similarly a compact subanalytic subset contained in one analytic chart has a finite compatible analytic partition, by bounded-chart comparison and finite cells. A connected cell lies in a single connected component; hence each component of a finite union of cells is a union of whole cells. There are finitely many components. For a compact subanalytic subset meeting several charts, intersect with finitely many compact coordinate boxes whose interiors cover it, apply the same finite-cell argument in each box, and take the resulting finite union of connected cells. This proves finiteness of its connected components as well.

The theorem supplies compatible analytic partitions and constant-rank refinements for the relative triangulation construction. Whitney and Verdier conditions and a frontier condition between partition members require additional arguments. The intrinsic analytic regular-locus theorem is established separately above.

Sources. Guillaume Valette, On subanalytic geometry, arXiv:2507.23622v1, §1.2, gives the graph/band cell definition and cell theorem; §2.1 gives first-order definable formulas and the definability of derivatives. The linked preparation component proves its finite-cell and Boolean/projection inputs in the stated projective product convention and retains its human credit and reuse terms. The manifold globalization, explicit derivative-limit formula, and simultaneous restriction-rank induction are written out here.

How a compatible triangulation is assembled

The triangulation input has a useful relative form: one may adapt a fixed locally finite polyhedron while preserving every old simplex setwise. Its geometric source is Masahiro Shiota, Piecewise Linearization of Real Analytic Functions, Proposition 3.1 and the closed-polyhedron form 3.1′, with Lemmas 3.2–3.7 and Remark 3.8. Shiota first chooses nonsingular projections, completes the finite graph families so that projection is open, and then straightens consecutive radial branches compatibly across faces. The proof below follows those mechanisms, spelling out the finite-jet argument for exceptional directions, the cap reflection, the reciprocal interpolation heights and the treatment of collapsed branch intervals. In particular, the inner simplex is chosen after graph completion; choosing it using only the original sets would not justify the subsequent graph ordering.

The lower subanalytic prerequisites used in this construction are uniformization, the set calculus, and the following forms of the regularity and dimension calculus. A nonempty subanalytic set has lower-dimensional frontier A¯\A\overline A\setminus A, as proved in Dimension, fibrewise closure and the frontier. This is distinct from the topological boundary, whose dimension can equal the dimension of the set. The compatible analytic partition theorem above proves that a locally finite family has a compatible locally finite partition into analytic submanifolds and that finitely many analytic maps have constant-rank restrictions after refinement. Compact subanalytic sets consequently have finite such partitions and finitely many connected components. These are inputs to the construction, rather than consequences of the triangulation being constructed. Analytic Noetherianity is supplied by the linked preparation proof. The analytic coordinate theorem gives constant-rank fibres and local analytic sections; the finite-system estimate (LAF9) proves the uniform zero-solution uniqueness used in the jet argument.

Relative polyhedron theorem. Let KK be a finite-dimensional locally finite linear simplicial complex with closed support in ℝN\mathbb R^N. Let {Ai}\{A_i\} be locally finite in the ambient space, with each AiA_i subanalytic and contained in |K||K|. There are a locally finite subdivision K′K' and a subanalytic homeomorphism

T:|K|⟶|K| T:|K|\longrightarrow |K|

such that T(σ)=σT(\sigma)=\sigma for every old closed simplex σ\sigma, each restriction to an open simplex of K′K' is an analytic diffeomorphism onto a subanalytic analytic submanifold, and every such image is contained in or disjoint from each AiA_i. No analyticity across simplex boundaries is asserted.

We first prove the ingredients that make the induction possible.

Choosing a point from which lines have finite intersections

Call a line singular for a set if it contains a nontrivial interval in that set. For a compact subanalytic set with no such intervals, every intersection with a line is finite: it is a compact zero-dimensional subanalytic set. For any countable collection of subanalytic sets of dimension less than nn, the union of their singular lines is meagre in ℝn\mathbb R^n. Their singular parallel directions form a meagre subset of ℝℙn−1\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}. Here, a meagre set is a countable union of nowhere dense sets.

Proof. A compatible analytic partition reduces the claim to countably many analytic submanifolds. A line interval in the original set contains an interval in one partition member: on a compact subinterval only finitely many members occur, and their intersections with the line are subanalytic. Work on a small open set where one such member is the zero set of an analytic function hh; a sum of squares of local defining functions supplies hh in higher codimension.

Choose analytic coordinates for a unit direction vv. Put L=v⋅∂xL=v\cdot\partial_x and gj=Ljhg_j=L^j h. The germ of the ascending chain of ideals (g0),(g0,g1),…(g_0),(g_0,g_1),\ldots stabilizes. Thus, on a neighborhood of any specified (x,v)(x,v), for some qq,

gq+1=∑j=0qaj(x,v)gj g_{q+1}=\sum_{j=0}^{q}a_j(x,v)g_j

with analytic coefficients. Along x+tvx+tv, the vector (g0,…,gq)(g_0,\ldots,g_q) satisfies a finite homogeneous linear differential system. If it is zero at t=0t=0, uniqueness makes it zero for all sufficiently small tt. Conversely, vanishing of h(x+tv)h(x+tv) on an interval makes all these initial jets zero. Hence the incidence of analytic line germs in the chosen submanifold is locally an analytic set defined by finitely many jet equations. This proves local finiteness of the equations; an infinite jet intersection has not been treated as automatically analytic.

Cover this incidence by countably many relatively compact closed subanalytic pieces and uniformize each piece. On its uniformizing manifold WW, write the analytic incidence parameters as x(w),v(w)x(w),v(w). The map

F:W×ℝ⟶ℝn,F(w,s)=x(w)+sv(w) F:W\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n, \qquad F(w,s)=x(w)+sv(w)

has rank less than nn for ss in a neighborhood of zero: locally its image lies in the lower-dimensional analytic zero set. At a fixed ww, every nn-rowed minor of its differential is a polynomial in ss, since its columns are dx+sdvdx+s\,dv and vv. Vanishing on an interval makes that polynomial identically zero. Thus FF has rank less than nn for every real ss, including values for which the line has left the original coordinate neighborhood.

Sard’s theorem makes the image measure zero. Exhaust W×ℝW\times\mathbb R by countably many compact sets. Each compact image is closed, has empty interior and is nowhere dense. This proves the assertion about all points on singular lines.

For directions, suppose w↦[v(w)]w\mapsto[v(w)] had surjective differential somewhere. A local analytic section over an open direction chart would give x=x(v)x=x(v). For the resulting map (v,s)↦x(v)+sv(v,s)\mapsto x(v)+sv, the determinant of its nn differential columns has leading coefficient

det⁡(∂1v,…,∂n−1v,v) \det(\partial_1v,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}v,v)

in its polynomial in ss. That coefficient is nonzero for a direction chart on the unit sphere. This contradicts the preceding rank calculation. The direction map therefore has only critical values. Sard and compact exhaustion again make its image meagre, now in projective space. In dimension one there are no line germs in a zero-dimensional set, so the assertion is immediate. Countable unions finish both claims. ▫\square

In particular, inside any open simplex one can choose a centre outside a finite family of compact lower-dimensional sets and all their singular lines. One can also choose a parallel direction avoiding all singular directions of such a family. Baire’s theorem gives the choices in any prescribed open neighborhood.

Completing a finite-fibre set so its projection is open

For p:ℝd×ℝ→ℝdp:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d, call a set projection-open when pp restricted to that set is an open map. Suppose AA is compact subanalytic and every vertical fibre is finite. A finite analytic partition of AA, compatible with a prescribed finite family of subsets, can be chosen in analytic graph pieces.

Proof of the graph assertion. Refine an analytic partition by the rank of pp. A constant-rank restriction cannot have rank smaller than the dimension of its partition member: the constant-rank theorem would give a positive-dimensional subset of a fibre. Remove the images of lower-dimensional pieces and frontiers, and partition the remaining image into connected analytic pieces. Over each such piece, compactness supplies a proper finite analytic covering. Its sheets have a canonical order in the last real coordinate. Following the first, second and subsequent values trivializes the covering, so each sheet is an analytic graph. Apply the same argument to the remaining lower-dimensional compact part. Dimension decreases strictly, and compactness gives finitely many pieces at every step. This yields the claimed finite graph partition. The properness used here is that of the projection on the compact closed set, including its frontier. ▫\square

There is a compact finite-fibre subanalytic enlargement B⊃AB\supset A that is projection-open near a specified point of AA.

Proof by induction on dd. The case d=0d=0 is immediate. Separate the dd-dimensional graph pieces, whose projection is open, from a closed compact remainder A2A_2 of dimension less than dd. Choose a parallel direction in the base that is nonsingular for p(A2)p(A_2), by the preceding lemma, and take it as the last base coordinate. For fixed x′∈ℝd−1x'\in\mathbb R^{d-1}, only finitely many base points (x′,xd)(x',x_d) occur in p(A2)p(A_2). Each has only finitely many heights. Thus the image of A2A_2 under

p2(x′,xd,y)=(x′,y) p_2(x',x_d,y)=(x',y)

has finite vertical fibres. Enlarge that compact image, by induction, to a set B2⊂ℝd−1×ℝB_2\subset\mathbb R^{d-1}\times\mathbb R whose projection is open near the specified point. Pull it back by p2p_2 and intersect with a sufficiently large closed ball. Near the specified point the ball has no effect. The resulting B′B' has finite vertical fibres and is projection-open; its projection has the free xdx_d-coordinate. It contains A2A_2. Therefore A∪B′A\cup B' is projection-open there: points of the remainder lie in the projection-open enlargement, while the other pieces already have open projection. This completes the induction. ▫\square

The same statements hold for radial projection from a centre aa, using polar coordinates away from aa. A local enlargement near b≠ab\ne a can be turned into a compact one that is projection-open everywhere without losing local membership data. Here is the boundary step. Rotate and scale so a=0a=0, b=(0,…,0,1)b=(0,\ldots,0,1). Intersect the local enlargement with a narrow conical neighborhood and a radial band about radius one. Choose the band endpoints to avoid its finite fibre over b/|b|b/|b|; narrow the cone so no points meet those radial endpoints. Its only boundary is then on the side of the cone. Reflect the spherical cap across its boundary sphere, leaving radial distance unchanged, and adjoin the reflected copy.

For completeness, such a reflection is analytic. Write a unit vector as (v′,vn)(v',v_n), let the cap boundary be vn=c∈(0,1)v_n=c\in(0,1), and put k=(1−c)/(1+c)>0k=(1-c)/(1+c)>0. The formula

J(v′,vn)=(2kv′1−vn+k2(1+vn),1−vn−k2(1+vn)1−vn+k2(1+vn)) J(v',v_n)=\left( \frac{2k\,v'}{1-v_n+k^2(1+v_n)}, \frac{1-v_n-k^2(1+v_n)}{1-v_n+k^2(1+v_n)} \right)

is an analytic involution of the sphere. Its denominator is positive; in stereographic coordinates it is inversion in the sphere of radius k\sqrt{k}. It fixes the cap boundary pointwise and exchanges its two sides. Near the common boundary, relative openness on the cap and its reflected copy gives openness in the whole sphere. The doubled compact set still has finite radial fibres. Partition it into graph pieces, also respecting its intersection with the original set and the cap boundary. Near bb, the original set is a union of these pieces. In dimension one radial directions form two points, and no cap construction is needed.

Extending the skeleton without changing old simplices

We prove the relative theorem by induction on m=dim⁡Km=\dim K. The assertion for m=0m=0 is immediate. Suppose it is proved in lower dimensions.

First reduce membership to closed sets. For a subanalytic AA in a compact old simplex, put B0=AB_0=A, Bj+1=Bj¯\BjB_{j+1}=\overline{B_j}\setminus B_j. The strict frontier inequality (D12) in the linked dimension provider makes this sequence terminate when the first empty set is reached. Membership in AA is a Boolean combination of the finitely many closed sets Bj¯\overline{B_j}, obtained by substituting Bj=Bj¯\Bj+1B_j=\overline{B_j}\setminus B_{j+1} backwards. For a full-dimensional closed set, its boundary is lower-dimensional; a connected piece avoiding that boundary lies wholly in its interior or wholly outside it. Thus lower-dimensional closed obstacles, and the membership information on the old skeleton, suffice. Each compact old simplex meets only finitely many AiA_i, so these local reductions preserve ambient local finiteness.

Fix an old mm-simplex σ\sigma, and choose a nonsingular centre a∈σ∘a\in\sigma^\circ outside its finite union of lower-dimensional closed obstacles. Such a choice is possible because that union and the excluded singular-line sets are meagre. Let pa:σ\{a}→∂σp_a:\sigma\setminus\{a\}\to\partial\sigma send a point along its ray to the boundary. Each obstacle has finite radial fibres. At each of its points use the preceding compact radial completion, with an analytic graph partition that records its local membership. Finitely many such neighborhoods cover the compact obstacles.

Let CC be the finite union of all the completed compact sets. Every completion was constructed away from aa, so CC is compact and avoids aa. Choose 0<δ<10<\delta<1 only now, small enough that the closed inner simplex a+δ(σ−a)a+\delta(\sigma-a) is disjoint from CC. Explicitly, if C≠⌀C\ne\varnothing, take δR<dist⁡(a,C)\delta R<\operatorname{dist}(a,C), where R=max⁡x∈σ|x−a|>0R=\max_{x\in\sigma}|x-a|>0; compactness makes the distance positive. If CC is empty, any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) suffices. Avoiding only the original obstacles would not ensure this property, because their completions can approach the centre more closely. Clip CC to σ\sigma, then add both ∂σ\partial\sigma and the inner boundary a+δ(∂σ−a)a+\delta(\partial\sigma-a). Call the resulting compact set Γ\Gamma. All completed points in it have radial height strictly greater than δ\delta, so the adjoined inner boundary is the least radial branch and the open inner simplex contains no other part of Γ\Gamma. It has finite radial fibres and open radial projection. Clipping does not spoil openness at an outer or inner boundary: the full boundary graph itself supplies the missing neighboring fibres.

Refine its finite graph partition to respect the partitions of every completion. Any connected piece compatible with this refinement is compatible with each original closed obstacle. Indeed, its intersection with that obstacle is closed. At an intersection point, a chosen completion neighborhood makes membership locally constant on the piece, so the intersection is also open. Connectedness makes it either the entire piece or empty.

Project all graph pieces and their relevant frontiers to the old skeleton, and include the original membership data on that skeleton. The images are subanalytic by properness on compact closures. The resulting family is locally finite: its members from σ\sigma remain on ∂σ\partial\sigma, and the old complex is locally finite. The induction hypothesis supplies a subdivision HH of the skeleton and a homeomorphism τ\tau that fixes every old face setwise, is analytic on each new open simplex, and respects this projected data.

Ordered branches, including their values on faces

Over an open base simplex η\eta of HH, after the boundary map τ\tau, the graph pieces of Γ\Gamma give finitely many strictly ordered positive radial functions

δ=r0(u)<r1(u)<⋯<rs(u)=1,u∈η∘, \delta=r_0(u)<r_1(u)<\cdots<r_s(u)=1, \qquad u\in\eta^\circ,

where the actual point on a branch is a+ri(u)(τ(u)−a)a+r_i(u)(\tau(u)-a). The functions are analytic on the open simplex. The boundary partition ensures that each branch either occurs on the entire base simplex or is absent there.

Each branch extends continuously to the closed base simplex. To see this at a boundary point u0u_0, intersect the open simplex with successively smaller balls centred at u0u_0. These intersections are connected. The closures of their branch graphs are nested compact connected sets. Their intersection is the cluster set over τ(u0)\tau(u_0), and is finite because Γ\Gamma has finite fibres. A nonempty finite connected set has one point. This gives a unique limiting value. The same argument at every boundary point, together with compactness, proves continuity of the extension.

On an open face, the limit is one of its finitely many graph branches. Its choice is locally constant, hence constant on the connected face. Consecutive branches upstairs restrict either to the same branch or to consecutive branches on a face. Otherwise a third branch strictly between their two limiting values would, by open projection, have nearby values over the interior base simplex. Those values would lie between the original consecutive branches, a contradiction. This is precisely where openness of the completed projection is needed.

Take a barycentric subdivision of HH. If two branches are distinct on an open base simplex, one vertex of each new simplex is the barycentre of its largest old carrier and lies in that carrier’s interior. Their values are strictly ordered at that vertex. They may agree at other vertices on lower faces; this causes a permitted collapse on that face, not a collapsed interior cell.

The straight model and its analytic lifting map

Let u0,…,udu_0,\ldots,u_d be the vertices of one of the subdivided base simplices, with barycentric coordinates λj(u)\lambda_j(u). Model branch ii by the straight simplex with vertices

a+ri(uj)(uj−a). a+r_i(u_j)(u_j-a).

Its radial height over uu is

Ri(u)=(∑j=0dλj(u)ri(uj))−1. R_i(u)=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{d}\frac{\lambda_j(u)}{r_i(u_j)}\right)^{-1}.

This is reciprocal, rather than arithmetic, interpolation. Indeed, if a point in the straight face has affine coefficients μj\mu_j, radial projection gives λj=μjri(uj)/t\lambda_j=\mu_jr_i(u_j)/t. The condition ∑μj=1\sum\mu_j=1 then gives the displayed height t=Ri(u)t=R_i(u). All vertex heights are positive. The strict order at an interior-carrier vertex makes Ri<Ri+1R_i<R_{i+1} throughout each open base simplex.

Between two consecutive straight faces, define

T(a+t(u−a))=a+[ri(u)+t−Ri(u)Ri+1(u)−Ri(u)(ri+1(u)−ri(u))](τ(u)−a). T\bigl(a+t(u-a)\bigr) =a+\left[ r_i(u)+\frac{t-R_i(u)}{R_{i+1}(u)-R_i(u)} \bigl(r_{i+1}(u)-r_i(u)\bigr) \right](\tau(u)-a).

On a straight branch use its endpoint value, and inside the inner simplex use the conical extension a+t(u−a)↦a+t(τ(u)−a)a+t(u-a)\mapsto a+t(\tau(u)-a), including a↦aa\mapsto a. The annular map is strictly increasing on each radial interval. On every open annular cell it is analytic with an analytic inverse: τ\tau and the branch functions are analytic there, radial projection is analytic on each old open face, and the radial derivative is

ri+1(u)−ri(u)Ri+1(u)−Ri(u)>0. \frac{r_{i+1}(u)-r_i(u)}{R_{i+1}(u)-R_i(u)}>0.

The maps agree on their common boundaries. If the two branches collapse on a lower face, every interpolated value lies between them, so continuity of their common limit supplies continuity there. There is no division by zero on an open annular cell. At the centre, the factor tt supplies continuity of the conical map. Thus TT is a homeomorphism of σ\sigma, agrees with τ\tau on its boundary, and takes straight branch faces and cells between them to the prescribed analytic branches and bands.

The straight faces and the closed regions between consecutive faces form a finite polyhedral cell complex. Over a fixed base face, their defining inequalities are the linear half-space inequalities of the two branch hyperplanes inside the cone over that face. The face restriction and consecutive-or-collapsed property just proved makes intersections common faces. A barycentric subdivision turns this into a simplicial subdivision. On every open simplex the restriction of the preceding analytic cell map is an analytic embedding, hence an analytic diffeomorphism onto its image.

The graph is subanalytic. On compact branch faces this follows from the subanalytic graph functions and τ\tau. For interpolation between two faces, take the closed subanalytic graph of the two endpoint maps over the same base ray, multiply by the compact parameter interval [0,1][0,1], and apply the analytic affine interpolation map to both its input and output coordinates. Its domain is compact, so this is a proper-image argument. The conical extension has the same compact graph construction, with the centre included. This avoids assuming that arbitrary nonproper compositions or images are subanalytic.

Do this on each old top simplex. The maps coincide on the skeleton, so they glue. Each map preserves its old simplex setwise. Local finiteness therefore gives a global homeomorphism, subanalytic graph and locally finite subdivision, with no accumulation of new cells in a compact neighborhood. Compatibility follows from the completed graph partition and the connected-piece argument. This proves the relative polyhedron theorem. ▫\square

Relative support and a continuous isotopy

The construction can preserve a region that already needs no change. Let LL be a subcomplex of KK, and suppose every old open simplex outside LL is already compatible with the family. All interior membership obstacles then lie in |L||L|. Their projected data stay in |L||L|, since every face of a simplex of LL belongs to LL. Inductively retain the old simplices disjoint from |L||L| and use the identity there. On a top simplex outside LL, the only remaining operation is conical extension of its already chosen boundary map. It is the identity when that closed simplex is disjoint from |L||L|. Thus the final subdivision retains those disjoint simplices and TT fixes them pointwise. This is the relative support refinement, not a claim that the map must fix every simplex merely absent from LL.

There is also a subanalytic isotopy from the identity to TT, preserving every old simplex setwise and stationary on those unchanged regions. Prove it with the same skeleton induction. Suppose τs\tau_s, 0≤s≤10\le s\le1, is the boundary isotopy. On an old top simplex let CτsC_{\tau_s} be its conical extension. Put D=Cτ1−1TD=C_{\tau_1}^{-1}T. This is an increasing homeomorphism on each radial fibre, fixes the outer boundary, and has the form

D(a+t(u−a))=a+q(u,t)(u−a). D(a+t(u-a))=a+q(u,t)(u-a).

Interpolate its radial coordinate by qs(u,t)=(1−s)t+sq(u,t)q_s(u,t)=(1-s)t+s\,q(u,t). Both summands are increasing, so qsq_s is strictly increasing, has the same endpoints and gives a fibre homeomorphism DsD_s. Define Ts=CτsDsT_s=C_{\tau_s}D_s. Then T0=idT_0=\mathrm{id}, T1=TT_1=T, and its boundary restriction is τs\tau_s. The formulas are continuous, including collapsed face intervals and the centre by the endpoint arguments above. On the compact old simplex, a continuous family of these bijections has a continuous family of inverses: the map (x,s)↦(Ts(x),s)(x,s)\mapsto(T_s(x),s) is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space. Its graph is subanalytic by the same compact interpolation constructions. Local finiteness glues the family over all old simplices. This proves the asserted subanalytic isotopy; no global analyticity across cells is implied.

An exact two-dimensional instance. The centre is a=(0,0)a=(0,0), the outer base is (u,1)(u,1), −1≤u≤1-1\le u\le1, and the target radial heights are r1(u)=1/3+u2/6r_1(u)=1/3+u^2/6, r2(u)=2/3+u2/6r_2(u)=2/3+u^2/6. Subdivide the base at u=0u=0. The corresponding straight-face heights are R1(u)=1/(3−|u|)R_1(u)=1/(3-|u|), R2(u)=10/(15−3|u|)R_2(u)=10/(15-3|u|). The displayed lifting map is affine along each ray between the two straight faces. Curves are shown through their stated exact parametrizations; the picture is a sampled illustration, not a substitute for the proof.

For the original manifold input, this proves the global Euclidean relative construction and its restriction to a closed subanalytic subset. The complete globalization to an arbitrary real analytic manifold is proved below through finite-colour chart blocks, differentiable subanalytic cutoffs and analytic coordinate recovery on open simplices. The lower subanalytic prerequisites stated at the start of the relative construction remain explicit.

The signed normal-cone prerequisite

For a closed analytic submanifold M⊂XM\subset X, the normal deformation 𝒟MX\mathcal D_MX has central fibre NMX=(TX|M)/TMN_MX=(TX|_M)/TM, a parameter ss, and a map p:𝒟MX→Xp:\mathcal D_MX\to X. In adapted coordinates (u,z)(u,z), with M={u=0}M=\{u=0\}, its maps are

p(v,z,s)=(sv,z),s(v,z,s)=s.(3) p(v,z,s)=(sv,z),\qquad s(v,z,s)=s. \qquad\text{(3)}

Put Ω={s>0}\Omega=\{s>0\}. For any subset A⊂XA\subset X, its normal cone is

CM(A)=NMX∩p−1(A)∩Ω¯.(4) C_M(A)=N_MX\cap\overline{p^{-1}(A)\cap\Omega}. \qquad\text{(4)}

The closure is taken in the deformation manifold. For locally closed MM, make this definition in an open ambient neighborhood where MM is closed. The normal-geometry locality comparison makes it independent of that choice.

For two subsets, the diagonal construction gives

C(A,B)=CΔ(A×B)⊂TX,[(v,w)]⟼v−w.(5) C(A,B)=C_\Delta(A\times B)\subset TX, \qquad [(v,w)]\longmapsto v-w. \qquad\text{(5)}

Thus the first member of the pair contributes with a plus sign. In a coordinate chart, the exact sequence criterion is

(x;v)∈C(A,B)⇔{aj∈A,bj∈B,aj,bj→x,cj>0,cj→∞,cj(aj−bj)→v.(6) (x;v)\in C(A,B) \iff \begin{cases} a_j\in A,\ b_j\in B,\quad a_j,b_j\to x,\\ c_j>0,\quad c_j\to\infty,\quad c_j(a_j-b_j)\to v. \end{cases} \qquad\text{(6)}

For Cx(A):=C{x}(A)C_x(A):=C_{\{x\}}(A), take bj=xb_j=x. The scale tending to infinity is also valid at the zero vector; it is part of the prerequisite criterion. Exchanging the two sets in (5) negates the cone. These are positive-conic sets, with no assumption that they are vector subspaces or convex.

Normal-cone subanalyticity. If AA is subanalytic and MM is an analytic submanifold, then CM(A)C_M(A) is subanalytic. If A,BA,B are subanalytic, then C(A,B)C(A,B) is subanalytic.

Proof. The maps in (3) are analytic. The lifted set p−1(A)∩{s>0}p^{-1}(A)\cap\{s>0\} is therefore subanalytic. Its closure and intersection with the analytic central fibre remain subanalytic by the set-operation input. For pairs, apply this argument to the diagonal and A×BA\times B; the latter is subanalytic by analytic inverse images and intersection. All assertions are local, so the same proof covers a locally closed MM. No image of a nonproper projection was used. ▫\square

A curve that represents the exact limiting vector

Curve realization. Let A,B⊂ℝnA,B\subset\mathbb R^n be subanalytic and v∈Cx(A,B)v\in C_x(A,B). There are analytic curve germs a(t),b(t)a(t),b(t), both equal to xx at zero, lying respectively in A,BA,B for nonzero tt, such that

a(t)−b(t)=tkv+O(tk+1)for some integer k>0.(7) a(t)-b(t)=t^k v+O(t^{k+1}) \quad\text{for some integer }k>0. \qquad\text{(7)}

The coefficient of vv in (7) is exactly one.

Proof. In ℝan×ℝyn×ℝs\mathbb R^n_a\times\mathbb R^n_y\times\mathbb R_s, consider

D={(a,y,s):s>0,a∈A,a−sy∈B}.(8) D=\{(a,y,s):s>0,\ a\in A,\ a-sy\in B\}. \qquad\text{(8)}

This is subanalytic by analytic inverse images and intersection. Criterion (6), with sj=cj−1s_j=c_j^{-1} and yj=cj(aj−bj)y_j=c_j(a_j-b_j), says that (x,v,0)∈D¯(x,v,0)\in\overline D. Curve selection gives analytic a(t),y(t),s(t)a(t),y(t),s(t) through that point and in DD for t≠0t\ne0. Set b(t)=a(t)−s(t)y(t)b(t)=a(t)-s(t)y(t). Both required set memberships hold, and b(0)=xb(0)=x.

The analytic function ss is positive on both sides of zero and vanishes at zero. Hence

s(t)=tkh(t),k≥2 even,h(0)>0.(9) s(t)=t^k h(t),\qquad k\ge2\text{ even},\quad h(0)>0. \qquad\text{(9)}

Choose the positive analytic kk-th root of hh near zero and put u=th(t)1/ku=t\,h(t)^{1/k}. Its derivative at zero is positive, so it has an analytic local inverse t=t(u)t=t(u). After this reparametrization, s(t(u))=uks(t(u))=u^k and y(t(u))=v+O(u)y(t(u))=v+O(u). The difference is therefore ukv+O(uk+1)u^k v+O(u^{k+1}), which is (7) after renaming the parameter. This also works for v=0v=0. The even exponent is a consequence of this particular two-sided construction; the theorem only needs a positive integer.

If curves on (−1,1)(-1,1) are desired, choose a small interval (−ε,ε)(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon) on which the germs are defined and compose them with t↦εtanh⁡(t/ε)t\mapsto\varepsilon\tanh(t/\varepsilon). This map takes (−1,1)(-1,1) into that interval and has Taylor expansion t+O(t3)t+O(t^3), so the coefficient and order in (7) are preserved. ▫\square

The rescaling in (9) matters. Without it, a selected curve initially gives ctkvc\,t^k v, with c=h(0)>0c=h(0)>0, and only a positive multiple of the specified leading vector has been normalized.

One-forms on a singular set

For an analytic one-form θ\theta on XX, define θ|S=0\theta|_S=0 to mean that its pullback to the analytic manifold SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} is zero. This restriction is on tangent vectors, rather than the assertion that the ambient covector θx\theta_x itself is zero.

Cone test. For a subanalytic set SS,

θ|S=0⇔θx(v)=0 for every x∈X and v∈Cx(S).(10) \theta|_S=0 \iff \theta_x(v)=0 \text{ for every }x\in X\text{ and }v\in C_x(S). \qquad\text{(10)}

This includes points in S¯\S\overline S\setminus S.

Proof. First we verify a density statement with its scales intact:

Cx(S)=Cx(Sreg).(11) C_x(S)=C_x(S_{\mathrm{reg}}). \qquad\text{(11)}

One inclusion follows from Sreg⊂SS_{\mathrm{reg}}\subset S. For the other, use a sequence zj∈Sz_j\in S and scales cj→∞c_j\to\infty representing a cone vector. Density of SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} in SS lets us choose wj∈Sregw_j\in S_{\mathrm{reg}} with ∥wj−zj∥<1/(jcj)\|w_j-z_j\|<1/(j c_j), in a fixed local chart for large jj. Then wj→xw_j\to x and cj(wj−x)−cj(zj−x)→0c_j(w_j-x)-c_j(z_j-x)\to0. This proves (11).

Suppose θ|S=0\theta|_S=0 and v≠0v\ne0 belongs to Cx(S)C_x(S). Apply (7) to SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} and {x}\{x\}, using (11). We obtain

a(t)=x+tkv+O(tk+1),a(t)∈Sreg(t≠0).(12) a(t)=x+t^k v+O(t^{k+1}),\qquad a(t)\in S_{\mathrm{reg}}\quad(t\ne0). \qquad\text{(12)}

At nonzero parameter the curve is tangent to SregS_{\mathrm{reg}}. Consequently θa(t)(ȧ(t))=0\theta_{a(t)}(\dot a(t))=0. Analytic Taylor expansion gives

0=ktk−1θx(v)+O(tk).(13) 0=k t^{k-1}\theta_x(v)+O(t^k). \qquad\text{(13)}

Divide by tk−1t^{k-1} and let t→0t\to0. The integer kk is nonzero, so θx(v)=0\theta_x(v)=0. The zero vector is automatic, and empty cone fibres make no demands.

Conversely, at a regular point xx, every tangent vector to SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} belongs to Cx(S)C_x(S): realize it by a smooth local curve and apply (6). Thus the right side of (10) kills every such tangent vector, which is the left side. ▫\square

For example, on the parabola S={(u,v):v=u2}S=\{(u,v):v=u^2\}, the nonzero ambient form dv−2ududv-2u\,du vanishes on SS. At the origin its value is dvdv, which kills the horizontal tangent cone. Vanishing on a set is consequently weaker than vanishing as a section of the ambient cotangent bundle.

Analytic maps and locally finite unions

Pullback and union rules. Let h:X′→Xh:X'\to X be analytic and let S′⊂X′S'\subset X', S⊂XS\subset X be subanalytic with h(S′)⊂Sh(S')\subset S. Then

θ|S=0⟹(h*θ)|S′=0.(14) \theta|_S=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(h^*\theta)|_{S'}=0. \qquad\text{(14)}

If {Si}\{S_i\} is locally finite and subanalytic, then vanishing on every SiS_i implies vanishing on ⋃iSi\bigcup_iS_i.

Proof. For v∈Cx′(S′)v\in C_{x'}(S'), take a sequence zj→x′z_j\to x' and scales cj→∞c_j\to\infty representing it. Taylor expansion at x′x' gives

cj(h(zj)−h(x′))⟶dhx′v.(15) c_j\bigl(h(z_j)-h(x')\bigr) \longrightarrow dh_{x'}v. \qquad\text{(15)}

Indeed, cj∥zj−x′∥c_j\|z_j-x'\| is bounded, so multiplying the first-order remainder o(∥zj−x′∥)o(\|z_j-x'\|) by cjc_j makes it tend to zero. Therefore dhx′v∈Ch(x′)(S)dh_{x'}v\in C_{h(x')}(S). The cone test yields (h*θ)x′(v)=θh(x′)(dhx′v)=0(h^*\theta)_{x'}(v)=\theta_{h(x')}(dh_{x'}v)=0, proving (14).

Near a fixed point, a locally finite union has only finitely many members. Its point-normal cone is the union of their point-normal cones, because closure commutes with a finite union in (4). Apply (10) to each member and then to the subanalytic union. ▫\square

In particular, vanishing passes to every subanalytic subset of SS, even a subset contained in its singular locus. This follows by taking hh to be the identity and S′⊂SS'\subset S.

Vanishing also passes to the closure. Here is the approximation argument, since uniformization applies to a closed set. For every ambient point xx,

Cx(S)=Cx(S¯). C_x(S)=C_x(\overline S).

The inclusion from left to right is immediate. For the reverse, represent a vector by zj∈S¯z_j\in\overline S, scales cj→∞c_j\to\infty, and cj(zj−x)→vc_j(z_j-x)\to v. Choose wj∈Sw_j\in S with ∥wj−zj∥<1/(jcj)\|w_j-z_j\|<1/(j c_j). Then wj→xw_j\to x and cj(wj−x)→vc_j(w_j-x)\to v. Both sets are subanalytic, so the cone test proves θ|S=0\theta|_S=0 if and only if θ|S¯=0\theta|_{\overline S}=0. This uses approximation at the chosen scales; density alone without that estimate would not identify the cones.

The reverse direction needs surjectivity onto the set, but does not need an everywhere surjective differential.

Surjective detection. Under the same assumptions, if h(S′)=Sh(S')=S, then

θ|S=0⟺(h*θ)|S′=0.(16) \theta|_S=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(h^*\theta)|_{S'}=0. \qquad\text{(16)}

Proof. Only detection remains. Set T=S′¯T=\overline{S'}. The closure argument just proved gives (h*θ)|T=0(h^*\theta)|_T=0. Choose a proper analytic uniformization π:W→X′\pi:W\to X' with image TT. The manifold WW, like our other manifolds, is Hausdorff and countable at infinity. By (14), (hπ)*θ=0(h\pi)^*\theta=0 on WW.

Fix a regular point of SS and a neighborhood VV in which S∩VS\cap V is a closed analytic manifold NN, of dimension dd. Shrink within that neighborhood if necessary. Then S¯∩V=N\overline S\cap V=N: taking closure introduces no new point inside a neighborhood where the set is already closed. Continuity gives h(T)⊂S¯h(T)\subset\overline S, whereas h(S′)=Sh(S')=S implies that h(T)h(T) contains SS. Consequently the following map is analytic and surjective:

g:(hπ)−1(V)⟶N,g=hπ.(17) g:(h\pi)^{-1}(V)\longrightarrow N, \qquad g=h\pi. \qquad\text{(17)}

The open source manifold has a countable atlas. The classical Sard theorem therefore makes its critical values a measure-zero subset in each chart of NN. Surjectivity implies that a dense set of points y∈Ny\in N has a lift zz with dgzdg_z onto TyNT_yN. At such a point, every w∈TyNw\in T_yN has a tangent lift vv, and

θy(w)=(g*θ)z(v)=0.(18) \theta_y(w)=(g^*\theta)_z(v)=0. \qquad\text{(18)}

Continuity makes θ|N\theta|_N zero everywhere. When d=0d=0 the conclusion already holds, since tangent spaces are zero. This works near every regular point of SS, proving (16). The differential-topology inputs are Sard and the usual submersion criterion. Properness is used for the available uniformization, not imposed on hh; we never assert that a nonproper analytic image is subanalytic. ▫\square

Generalized conormals retain limiting normal covectors

For a locally closed subanalytic S⊂XS\subset X, define

TS*X=TSreg*X¯∩π−1(S),π:T*X→X.(19) T_S^*X =\overline{T_{S_{\mathrm{reg}}}^*X}\cap\pi^{-1}(S), \qquad \pi:T^*X\to X. \qquad\text{(19)}

The ordinary conormal on the right kills the tangent space of the regular locus. Its closure retains limiting covectors, while the last intersection restricts their base points back to SS. Formula (19) need not give the annihilator of Cx(S)C_x(S) at a singular point.

Generalized-conormal subanalyticity. The set TS*XT_S^*X is subanalytic.

Proof. Work in an ambient open set where SS is closed, and choose a proper uniformization f:Y→Xf:Y\to X with image SS. Let

Y0={y∈f−1(Sreg):dfy:TyY→Tf(y)Sreg is onto},S0=f(Y0).(20) Y_0=\{y\in f^{-1}(S_{\mathrm{reg}}): df_y:T_yY\to T_{f(y)}S_{\mathrm{reg}} \text{ is onto}\},\qquad S_0=f(Y_0). \qquad\text{(20)}

Here Y0Y_0 is subanalytic. For each possible dimension dd of the regular locus, intersect its inverse image with {rank⁡df=d}\{\operatorname{rank}df=d\}. The regular dimension parts are subanalytic, and the rank conditions are semianalytic minors. Near a point mapping to the regular locus, the image of dfdf is tangent to that locus, so rank dd is exactly the surjectivity in (20).

The set Y0Y_0 is open in YY, because SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} is open in SS and surjectivity is open over a fixed-dimensional manifold. Properness of ff implies properness on Y0¯\overline{Y_0}, so S0S_0 is subanalytic. The submersion theorem makes S0S_0 open in SregS_{\mathrm{reg}}. It is dense there: over any regular neighborhood, ff is a surjective analytic map onto that neighborhood, and Sard shows that regular values are dense. Thus S0S_0 is also dense in SS.

Use the typed cotangent correspondence

C=Y×XT*X,fπ:C→T*X,fd:C→T*Y,fd(y;ξ)=dfytξ.(21) C=Y\times_XT^*X, \qquad f_\pi:C\to T^*X, \qquad f_d:C\to T^*Y, \quad f_d(y;\xi)=df_y^t\xi. \qquad\text{(21)}

The first map is a base change of the proper map ff; hence it is proper on all of CC. Let Ṫ*Y0\dot T^*Y_0 denote the nonzero covectors over Y0Y_0, as a subanalytic subset of T*YT^*Y, and set

P=T*X\fπ(fd−1(Ṫ*Y0)).(22) P=T^*X\setminus f_\pi\bigl(f_d^{-1}(\dot T^*Y_0)\bigr). \qquad\text{(22)}

Analytic inverse image, proper image and difference prove that PP is subanalytic. Explicitly, (x;ξ)∈P(x;\xi)\in P means that dfytξ=0df_y^t\xi=0 for every y∈Y0∩f−1(x)y\in Y_0\cap f^{-1}(x). Over S0S_0 at least one such lift exists and every such differential is onto TxSregT_xS_{\mathrm{reg}}. Consequently

P∩π−1(S0)=TS0*X.(23) P\cap\pi^{-1}(S_0)=T_{S_0}^*X. \qquad\text{(23)}

The two conormal bundles over S0S_0 and SregS_{\mathrm{reg}} have the same closure. To see the nontrivial inclusion, choose local conormal-bundle coordinates around a regular point, approximate its base point by points of the dense open S0S_0, and keep the normal-fibre coordinates fixed. Every regular conormal covector is then a limit from TS0*XT_{S_0}^*X. Taking closure in (23) and intersecting with π−1(S)\pi^{-1}(S) proves (19) subanalytic. The normal-cone arguments earlier supplied a different construction; no equality between these two kinds of cone was assumed. ▫\square

At the crossing S={uv=0}⊂ℝ2S=\{uv=0\}\subset\mathbb R^2, the generalized-conormal fibre at the origin is the union of the two covector axes. The point-normal cone is the union of the two tangent axes; the covectors annihilating all of it consist only of zero. These two answers encode different questions. A subsequent stratification includes the origin as its own stratum, whose ordinary conormal is the entire cotangent fibre.

Exercises with solutions

Two notions of a normal covector

Difficulty: Intermediate.

Compute (TS*ℝ2)0(T_S^*\mathbb R^2)_0 and the annihilator of C0(S)C_0(S) for S={uv=0}S=\{uv=0\}. Then compute TA*ℝT_A^*\mathbb R for A=[0,∞)A=[0,\infty). Compare its fibre at zero with the conormal of the point stratum.

Solution. Away from zero, the horizontal axis has conormal ξ=0\xi=0, and the vertical axis has conormal η=0\eta=0, where a covector is ξdu+ηdv\xi\,du+\eta\,dv.
