Their closures give {ξ=0}∪{η=0}\{\xi=0\}\cup\{\eta=0\} at zero. Every scaled displacement in SS lies on a tangent axis, and every vector on either axis is attained. Thus C0(S)C_0(S) is their union. A covector killing both axes has ξ=η=0\xi=\eta=0.

For AA, the regular locus is (0,∞)(0,\infty), whose conormal is the zero covector. Its closure, restricted to AA, is the zero section over [0,∞)[0,\infty). In particular, (19) gives only zero at the endpoint. The conormal of {0}⊂ℝ\{0\}\subset\mathbb R is the whole one-dimensional fibre. The stratified conormal union therefore contains more endpoint covectors than the generalized conormal of the entire half-line.

A two-sided curve in a one-sided cone

Difficulty: Introductory.

Let A=(0,∞)⊂ℝA=(0,\infty)\subset\mathbb R. Compute C0(A)C_0(A). For every v>0v>0, give an analytic curve in AA for both signs of its nonzero parameter with leading coefficient vv. Explain why a nonzero first-order term cannot work.

Solution. Positive scales of positive points are positive, so every limiting vector is nonnegative. Conversely aj=v/ja_j=v/j, cj=jc_j=j realize v>0v>0, while aj=1/j2a_j=1/j^2, cj=jc_j=j realize zero. Hence C0(A)=[0,∞)C_0(A)=[0,\infty). The curve a(t)=vt2a(t)=v t^2 has exactly the required coefficient and belongs to AA for every nonzero tt. A real analytic function with nonzero linear term changes sign across zero. It therefore cannot remain in AA on both sides.

Quadratic tangency enlarges a pair cone

Difficulty: Advanced.

At the origin, compute C(A,B)C(A,B) for A={(u,u2):u∈ℝ}A=\{(u,u^2):u\in\mathbb R\} and B={(u,0):u∈ℝ}B=\{(u,0):u\in\mathbb R\}. Compare it with the difference of their tangent spaces. Realize every vector in the answer by two analytic curves as in (7).

Solution. A difference from AA to BB has nonnegative vertical coordinate, and positive scaling preserves it. Therefore the cone is contained in ℝ×[0,∞)\mathbb R\times[0,\infty). Given (a,b)(a,b) with b>0b>0, use

a1(t)=(bt,bt2),b1(t)=(bt−at2,0).(24) a_1(t)=(\sqrt b\,t,b t^2),\qquad b_1(t)=(\sqrt b\,t-a t^2,0). \qquad\text{(24)}

They lie in the respective sets and their difference is t2(a,b)t^2(a,b). For b=0b=0, take a1(t)=(0,0)a_1(t)=(0,0) and b1(t)=(−at2,0)b_1(t)=(-a t^2,0). Evaluating at t=1/jt=1/j with scale j2j^2 proves the reverse inclusion, including the zero vector. Both tangent spaces at the origin are horizontal, so their difference is only the horizontal line. The pair cone also sees the second-order separation. Reversing the ordered pair gives ℝ×(−∞,0]\mathbb R\times(-\infty,0].

An analytic image that escapes the properness hypothesis

Difficulty: Intermediate.

Show that the image of f:ℝ→ℝ2f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2, f(t)=(e−t,sin⁡t)f(t)=(e^{-t},\sin t), is not subanalytic in ℝ2\mathbb R^2. Identify a compact set whose inverse image proves that ff is not proper.

Solution. If the image were subanalytic, its intersection with the analytic line {y=0}\{y=0\} would be subanalytic. That intersection is

{(e−mπ,0):m∈ℤ}.(25) \{(e^{-m\pi},0):m\in\mathbb Z\}. \qquad\text{(25)}

Each member is an isolated connected component. Infinitely many approach the ambient point (0,0)(0,0), so these components are not locally finite there. This contradicts the connected-component theorem, even though the accumulation point is not in the image. The compact rectangle [0,1]×[−1,1][0,1]\times[-1,1] has inverse image [0,∞)[0,\infty), which is noncompact. Thus the proper-image theorem does not apply.

Detection through a critical point

Difficulty: Introductory.

Let h(t)=t3h(t)=t^3 and θ=a(x)dx\theta=a(x)\,dx, with aa analytic on ℝ\mathbb R. Prove directly that h*θ=0h^*\theta=0 implies θ=0\theta=0, although dh0=0dh_0=0. Give a failure of detection when surjectivity onto the specified set is dropped.

Solution. The pullback is 3t2a(t3)dt3t^2a(t^3)\,dt. Its vanishing gives a(t3)=0a(t^3)=0 for t≠0t\ne0. Every nonzero xx is a nonzero cube, and continuity gives a(0)=0a(0)=0 as well. Therefore θ=0\theta=0. For failure, take a constant map h:ℝ→ℝh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R, h(t)=0h(t)=0, and specify S′=S=ℝS'=S=\mathbb R. Then h*dx=0h^*dx=0 whereas dx|S≠0dx|_S\ne0. Its image is {0}\{0\}, rather than SS.

A connected subanalytic set cannot vary under a vanishing differential

Difficulty: Advanced.

Let S⊂XS\subset X be connected and subanalytic, and let g:X→ℝg:X\to\mathbb R be analytic with dg|S=0dg|_S=0. Prove that gg is constant on SS, without a properness assumption on gg.

Solution. The empty case is vacuous. The closure consequence of the cone test gives dg|S¯=0dg|_{\overline S}=0. Uniformize that closed set by a proper analytic π:W→X\pi:W\to X. Rule (14) gives d(gπ)=0d(g\pi)=0 on WW, so gπg\pi is constant on each connected component. A second-countable manifold has at most countably many components: each is open and contains a member of a fixed countable basis, and different components contain different such members. Thus g(S¯)g(\overline S), and hence g(S)g(S), is countable. It is connected because gg is continuous and SS is connected. A connected subset of ℝ\mathbb R containing two different points contains the interval between them, which is uncountable. Hence g(S)g(S) contains one point. This proof uses neither subanalyticity of g(S)g(S) nor properness of gg, and needs no triangulation.

Division at a normal-crossing boundary

Difficulty: Advanced.

Near (0,0)(0,0), let A,C,BA,C,B be analytic functions and put r=u2v3r=u^2v^3, α=Adu+Cdv\alpha=A\,du+C\,dv. Suppose rα+Bdr=0r\alpha+B\,dr=0 as an analytic one-form. Show that B=uvHB=uvH for an analytic HH, and that BB and the tangential restriction of α\alpha vanish on the normal-crossing set {uv=0}\{uv=0\}.

Solution. Comparing coefficients and cancelling analytic factors in the local ring gives

uA+2B=0,vC+3B=0.(26) uA+2B=0,\qquad vC+3B=0. \qquad\text{(26)}

Thus both uu and vv divide BB. Expand BB as a convergent power series: divisibility by uu removes all terms of uu-degree zero and divisibility by vv removes all terms of vv-degree zero. Factoring uvuv leaves a convergent analytic series HH. Equations (26) give A=−2vHA=-2vH, C=−3uHC=-3uH. Hence B=0B=0 on both axes. Along {u=0}\{u=0\} the tangent differential is dvdv, whose coefficient CC is zero; along {v=0}\{v=0\} it is dudu, whose coefficient AA is zero. These are exactly the restrictions on the regular locus of the crossing. The cone test supplies the same vanishing at its singular point. This is the local division mechanism used when a resolved analytic function has monomial zeros.

Absorbing a unit while preserving two boundary axes

Difficulty: Intermediate.

For φ(u,v)=−evu2v3\varphi(u,v)=-e^v u^2v^3 near (0,0)(0,0), give analytic coordinates expressing φ\varphi as a sign times a monomial. Verify invertibility and preservation of both zero-set axes. Explain why the same coordinate step cannot make the nonconstant function eve^v into the monomial with every exponent zero.

Solution. Put z1=ev/2uz_1=e^{v/2}u, z2=vz_2=v. Then φ=−z12z23\varphi=-z_1^2z_2^3. The Jacobian determinant is ev/2e^{v/2}, which is positive; the inverse is u=e−z2/2z1u=e^{-z_2/2}z_1, v=z2v=z_2. Thus both axes and their crossing remain the same sets. An all-zero-exponent monomial is constant. If eve^v became constant after a coordinate change with an inverse, composing back would make eve^v constant on an open neighborhood, contradicting its nonzero vv-derivative. The point of the unit lemma is the available positive exponent at a zero, not an assertion that every unit is constant in suitable coordinates.

Centres, parallel directions and a projection-open enlargement

Difficulty: Intermediate.

Let AA be the union of the two axis segments in [−1,1]2[-1,1]^2. Determine its singular lines, choose a centre from which every line has finite intersection with AA, and choose a good parallel direction. Then explain why the projection of the one-point set {(0,0)}\{(0,0)\} to the first coordinate is not open and give a compact finite-fibre enlargement whose projection is open near that point.

Solution. An interval in AA lies on one of its axes, so the only singular lines are the two coordinate axes. Any centre with both coordinates nonzero, for example (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2), lies on neither; a line through it cannot coincide with an axis and meets the two segments in at most two points. The direction (1,1)(1,1) is nonsingular for every translate: its lines are parallel to neither axis. In contrast, either axis direction has a singular translate. The image of the one-point set is {0}\{0\}, which is not open in the base line, although the singleton is open in its own subspace topology. The enlargement [−1,1]×{0}[-1,1]\times\{0\} has one-point vertical fibres and open projection near the origin. Projection openness is local here; at its two endpoints the map to the whole base line is not open. The example also shows that an enlargement may have larger dimension than the original set.

Reciprocal heights and the exact radial lift

Difficulty: Advanced.

Use the two target branches in the figure, with base subdivided at u=0u=0. Compute the straight heights on 0≤u≤10\le u\le1. On the ray u=1/2u=1/2, compute the domain and image of the midpoint between the two straight faces under the lifting map. Explain why averaging the vertex heights would not describe a straight face.

Solution. On that base interval the vertex weights are 1−u,u1-u,u. The lower vertex heights are 1/3,1/21/3,1/2, and the upper ones are 2/3,5/62/3,5/6. Therefore

R1(u)=13−u,R2(u)=1(3/2)(1−u)+(6/5)u=1015−3u. R_1(u)=\frac{1}{3-u},\qquad R_2(u)=\frac{1}{(3/2)(1-u)+(6/5)u} =\frac{10}{15-3u}.

At u=1/2u=1/2, these are 2/5,20/272/5,20/27, and their midpoint is 77/13577/135. Thus the domain point is p=(77/270,77/135)p=(77/270,77/135). The target heights are 3/8,17/243/8,17/24. Since the map is affine on this radial interval, its midpoint has height 13/2413/24, giving T(p)=(13/48,13/24)T(p)=(13/48,13/24). Both points lie on the ray with base (1/2,1)(1/2,1). The arithmetic average of the lower vertex heights is 5/125/12, whereas the straight face has radial height 2/52/5. The difference comes from radial projection: the affine coefficients of a point in the straight face are proportional to λj/rj\lambda_j/r_j, rather than to the base weights λj\lambda_j themselves. This is the reciprocal-height calculation in the proof.

Resolving a function whose real zero set already crosses normally

Difficulty: Advanced.

For φ(x,y)=xy(x2+y2)\varphi(x,y)=xy(x^2+y^2), compute Z={φ=0,dφ=0}Z=\{\varphi=0,d\varphi=0\}. Let

Y={((x,y),[α:β])∈ℝ2×ℝℙ1:xβ=yα},f((x,y),[α:β])=(x,y). Y=\{((x,y),[\alpha:\beta])\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb{RP}^1: x\beta=y\alpha\}, \qquad f((x,y),[\alpha:\beta])=(x,y).

Prove that YY is an analytic manifold, that ff is proper and is an analytic isomorphism over ℝ2\Z\mathbb R^2\setminus Z, and that φ∘f\varphi\circ f has the required sign-monomial coordinates near every point of f−1Zf^{-1}Z.

Solution. The derivatives are

∂xφ=y(3x2+y2),∂yφ=x(x2+3y2). \partial_x\varphi=y(3x^2+y^2),\qquad \partial_y\varphi=x(x^2+3y^2).

The real zero set consists of the axes. On y=0y=0, the second derivative is x3x^3; on x=0x=0, the first is y3y^3. Thus the zero-critical set is exactly Z={(0,0)}Z=\{(0,0)\}.

On the projective chart α≠0\alpha\ne0, put v=β/αv=\beta/\alpha and u=xu=x. The incidence relation says y=uvy=uv, so (u,v)(u,v) are unrestricted analytic coordinates. On β≠0\beta\ne0, put s=α/βs=\alpha/\beta and w=yw=y; there x=swx=sw, with analytic coordinates (s,w)(s,w). On their overlap the transition is

s=1/v,w=uv, s=1/v,\qquad w=uv,

with nonzero determinant 1/v1/v. These charts cover YY, including its whole exceptional fibre over the origin. They make it an analytic two-manifold and make ff analytic.

The incidence set is closed in ℝ2×ℝℙ1\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb{RP}^1: in each projective chart it is the zero set of the displayed continuous equation, so its complement is open. The projective line is compact, being the quotient of the unit circle by its antipodal involution. For compact C⊂ℝ2C\subset\mathbb R^2, the set f−1(C)f^{-1}(C) is consequently closed in the compact product C×ℝℙ1C\times\mathbb{RP}^1 and is compact. Hence ff is proper. It is surjective; the origin has a projective line of preimages, and each nonzero (x,y)(x,y) has the unique preimage with direction [x:y][x:y]. The inverse (x,y)↦((x,y),[x:y])(x,y)\mapsto((x,y),[x:y]) is analytic on the punctured plane, as one sees on x≠0x\ne0 and y≠0y\ne0. This proves the isomorphism over precisely the required complement.

In the first chart,

φ∘f=u4v(1+v2). \varphi\circ f=u^4v(1+v^2).

At the exceptional point (u,v)=(0,0)(u,v)=(0,0), set U=u(1+v2)1/4U=u(1+v^2)^{1/4}, V=vV=v. The Jacobian determinant there is one, the axes are preserved, and φ∘f=U4V\varphi\circ f=U^4V. At (0,v0)(0,v_0) with v0≠0v_0\ne0, let ε=sign⁡(v0)\varepsilon=\operatorname{sign}(v_0) and shrink so that vv keeps this sign. Use coordinates

U=u|v(1+v2)|1/4,V=v−v0. U=u\,|v(1+v^2)|^{1/4},\qquad V=v-v_0.

The root is positive and analytic, the Jacobian determinant at the point is |v0(1+v02)|1/4>0|v_0(1+v_0^2)|^{1/4}>0, and φ∘f=εU4\varphi\circ f=\varepsilon U^4.

The second chart supplies the remaining direction [α:β]=[0:1][\alpha:\beta]=[0:1]:

φ∘f=sw4(1+s2). \varphi\circ f=sw^4(1+s^2).

At (s,w)=(0,0)(s,w)=(0,0), set S=sS=s, W=w(1+s2)1/4W=w(1+s^2)^{1/4}, giving SW4SW^4 with invertible Jacobian. If s0≠0s_0\ne0, set S=s−s0S=s-s_0, W=w|s(1+s2)|1/4W=w|s(1+s^2)|^{1/4}; the expression becomes sign⁡(s0)W4\operatorname{sign}(s_0)W^4. Thus every point of f−1Zf^{-1}Z has a sign-only coordinate monomial. Only the two axis directions require two positive exponents; every other exceptional direction requires one. The real zero-set picture had concealed the extra vanishing factor, and the complete two-chart construction retains it.

Coefficients, a cusp and an unresolved exceptional tangency

Level: advanced. For h(x,t)=t2−x3h(x,t)=t^2-x^3 marked with 22, compute its coefficient conditions, the two charts of the blowing-up of the origin, and the order at the exceptional points. Explain why the first multiplicity drop does not yet give normal crossings of the total function divisor.

Solution. The distinguished derivative is ∂t2h=2\partial_t^2h=2; N={t=0}N=\{t=0\}, c0=−x3c_0=-x^3 with mark 22, and c1=0c_1=0 with mark 11. The coefficient order is at least two only at x=0x=0, so the equimultiple locus is the origin. The coefficient’s normalized order there is 3/23/2.

In the xx chart, x=u,t=uvx=u,t=uv. The total and controlled transforms are

h∘σ=u2(v2−u),h′=v2−u. h\circ\sigma=u^2(v^2-u),\qquad h'=v^2-u.

The transformed coefficient is −u-u with mark 22, exactly (−u3)/u2(-u^3)/u^2, so its order has dropped below its mark. At the exceptional point (0,0)(0,0), h′h' has order one because ∂uh′=−1\partial_u h'=-1. At an exceptional point (0,v0)(0,v_0) with v0≠0v_0\ne0, h′h' is a unit. In the tt chart, t=w,x=wzt=w,x=wz, the controlled transform is 1−wz31-wz^3; it is a unit on the entire exceptional line w=0w=0. These computations cover every projective direction.

The strict transform u=v2u=v^2 is smooth but tangent to the exceptional line u=0u=0 at the origin. Their differentials there are proportional. Thus their union is not normal crossing, despite the distinguished multiplicity having dropped from two to one. The total transform retains the exceptional exponent two. Both the exceptional-incidence conditions and the coefficient weights must remain visible in the resolution algorithm.

The necessary gradient exponent on a flat direction

Level: intermediate. For f(x,y)=x2+y4f(x,y)=x^2+y^4, prove a local Łojasiewicz gradient inequality with exponent 3/43/4, and show that a smaller exponent cannot hold in any neighborhood of the origin.

Solution. The Euclidean gradient is (2x,4y3)(2x,4y^3). For |x|,|y|≤1|x|,|y|\le1, concavity of the power r3/4r^{3/4} gives

f3/4≤|x|3/2+|y|3≤|x|+|y|3≤34|∇f|. f^{3/4}\le |x|^{3/2}+|y|^3 \le |x|+|y|^3 \le \frac34|\nabla f|.

For completeness, subadditivity (a+b)p≤ap+bp(a+b)^p\le a^p+b^p, 0<p<10<p<1, follows by fixing a≥0a\ge0 and differentiating (a+b)p−bp(a+b)^p-b^p for b>0b>0: its derivative is nonpositive, so its value is at most apa^p. The last inequality uses |∇f|≥2|x||\nabla f|\ge2|x| and |∇f|≥4|y|3|\nabla f|\ge4|y|^3.

On x=0,y≠0x=0,y\ne0, an inequality fρ≤C|∇f|f^\rho\le C|\nabla f| would require |y|4ρ−3≤4C|y|^{4\rho-3}\le4C. If ρ<3/4\rho<3/4, its left side tends to infinity as y→0y\to0, which is impossible. Thus the flat direction determines the necessary exponent. The full gradient theorem in the human component explains why some rational exponent below one exists; this calculation determines the optimal exponent for this function.

Formal replacement and signed analytic normalization

Exercise 14 (intermediate). Explain why the formal linear convergence theorem does not claim convergence of every formal solution. Give a divergent formal solution of f1−f2=1f_1-f_2=1 in ℝ[[x]]\mathbb R[[x]], and a convergent solution with the same jet through any fixed degree. For ψ(u,z)=u−z\psi(u,z)=u-z, |u|≤1|u|\le1, normalize by the coefficient of largest absolute value, using the zz coefficient at a tie. Determine the normalizing parameters and a uniform bound on the order in zz.

Solution. Let

ĥ(x)=∑n≥0n!xn,(f̂1,f̂2)=(1+ĥ,ĥ). \widehat h(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}n!x^n,\qquad (\widehat f_1,\widehat f_2)=(1+\widehat h,\widehat h).

The difference is 11 coefficientwise. For any x≠0x\ne0, the absolute terms of ĥ\widehat h have ratio (n+1)|x|(n+1)|x|, which eventually exceeds two. They therefore do not tend to zero, so this series has convergence radius zero. Both components of the displayed formal solution diverge.

For any fixed q≥0q\ge0, put pq(x)=∑n=0qn!xnp_q(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{q}n!x^n. The pair (1+pq,pq)(1+p_q,p_q) is a polynomial solution and agrees with the formal pair in degrees 0,…,q0,\ldots,q. Thus a convergent replacement can preserve every prescribed finite jet, although there is no single convergent series with all those Taylor coefficients. The distinction persists even for this elementary finite linear equation.

For the second part, c0=uc_0=u, c1=−1c_1=-1, and the units are A0=A1=1A_0=A_1=1. On |u|≤1|u|\le1, take m=1m=1, gm=−1g_m=-1. Then

t0=−u,t1=1,Q(t,u,z)=t0+t1z=−u+z,ψ(u,z)=(−1)Q(t,u,z). t_0=-u,\qquad t_1=1,\qquad Q(t,u,z)=t_0+t_1z=-u+z,\qquad \psi(u,z)=(-1)Q(t,u,z).

The first parameter takes both signs. Restricting it to [0,1][0,1] would omit positive uu. On the correct signed compact interval, ∂zQ=1\partial_zQ=1 everywhere. Therefore the order is at most one uniformly; at z=uz=u it is exactly one, and elsewhere it is zero. This verifies the derivative criterion even where the normalized value itself vanishes.

References and the next cotangent question

Bierstone–Milman, Semianalytic and subanalytic sets, Definition 3.1 and §§3, 5 and 7, treats the local projection language, complement theorem, proper uniformization and fixed-dimensional regularity. Proposition 3.12, printed pp. 19–20, gives a dimension-preserving analytic presentation. Theorem 5.1, pp. 30–32, proves analytic-set uniformization using normal-crossing charts and induction through lower-dimensional centres; the deduction for closed subanalytic sets follows on p. 32. The torus argument here uses a compact fibre extremum and squared differential minors to reduce the source dimension directly from the proved function resolution. The uniformization conclusion supplies a proper map onto the set; the separate function-resolution theorem also retains its asserted isomorphism away from the singular zero set.

Valette’s On subanalytic geometry, §1.2 and §§2.1–2.2, supplies finite analytic cells, definable derivative tests and the choice-plus-Puiseux route to analytic curves in the globally subanalytic setting. The bounded-chart comparison is what permits their use on the local sets here. The two-sided curve and exact leading-vector normalizations are then checked in this lesson. The linked adapted components retain Valette’s attribution and CC BY 4.0 terms.

Shiota’s relative polyhedron proof is the triangulation source described above. The later manifold argument proves its globalization through finite-colour chart blocks, finite-regularity subanalytic cutoffs and analytic coordinate recovery on open simplices; its specific Kankaanrinta and Milnor credits appear at those constructions. The arbitrary-manifold conclusion is therefore proved here from the stated lower inputs. The separate function-resolution proof proceeds through the marked coefficient construction, recursive exceptional histories, analytic thresholds, closed canonical centres, compact-fibre termination, and proper gluing of the independently matched local towers.

For the cotangent setting, Kashiwara–Schapira’s freely readable Microlocal Study of Sheaves, §§8.1–8.2 explains how Whitney limits control conormals and how isotropic sets lie in conormal unions. Its §8.2 convention restricts “subanalytic set” to locally closed sets, so it is not a substitute for the arbitrary-subset calculus used here. Our closure and surjective-detection proofs retain that broader stated scope and use the explicit curve and uniformization inputs; they do not require triangulation.

Guillaume Valette’s On subanalytic geometry, §2.2, supplies the separately licensed choice, curve-selection and Łojasiewicz treatment linked above. The linked analytic preparation treatment now proves its Chapter1 cell, complement and Puiseux inputs in the projective product convention. The local comparison here proves the manifold curve-selection consequence without a global definability assumption. The marked coefficient argument proves the local dimension reduction and its test-transform persistence. Higher analytic prefixes, current history, and rebirth supplies the recursive exceptional histories, and Finite termination over a compact fibre proves termination for the local towers used in the proper global construction.

For the next step, take the canonical one-form on T*XT^*X. Its vanishing on a positive-conic subanalytic set defines isotropy. The cone test and surjective detection just proved will then turn cotangent correspondences into rigorous statements about isotropic images and stratifications.

Further exercises on preparation

15. A bounded function that needs a negative preparation exponent

Level: advanced. On

C={(x,y):0<x<ϵ,x2<y<x},0<ϵ<1, C=\{(x,y):0<x<\epsilon,\ x^2<y<x\},\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,

consider f(x,y)=x3/yf(x,y)=x^3/y. It is positive and bounded. Show that a finite preparation of ff cannot have only nonnegative last-coordinate exponents, even if translations and analytic units are allowed. Use the convergent Puiseux theorem proved in the analytic preparation treatment.

Solution. We have 0<f<x<ϵ0<f<x<\epsilon. The formula f=x3y−1f=x^3y^{-1} is already a reduction with translation zero, unit one and exponent −1-1.

Suppose there is a finite cell preparation with all exponents nonnegative. Refine its one-dimensional base and shrink ϵ\epsilon so its base interval next to zero is (0,ϵ)(0,\epsilon). Over it, list the finitely many endpoints within the original band, including x2x^2 and xx:

x2=α0(x)<α1(x)<⋯<αN(x)=x. x^2=\alpha_0(x)<\alpha_1(x)<\cdots<\alpha_N(x)=x.

Duplicate endpoints are removed; every open interval between consecutive endpoints is a preparation cell. Each positive endpoint has a convergent Puiseux expansion with leading term cjxνjc_jx^{\nu_j}, where cj>0c_j>0. The bounds x2≤αj≤xx^2\le\alpha_j\le x force 1≤νj≤21\le\nu_j\le2. Since ν0=2\nu_0=2 and νN=1\nu_N=1, some consecutive pair α<β\alpha<\beta has strictly decreasing leading order. Thus α/β→0\alpha/\beta\to0.

On the corresponding band, write the supposed reduction as

f(x,y)=a(x)|y−θ(x)|rU(x,y),r≥0,0<m≤|U|≤M. f(x,y)=a(x)|y-\theta(x)|^rU(x,y),\qquad r\ge0, \qquad 0<m\le|U|\le M.

The coefficient cannot vanish, since f>0f>0. The center is outside the band, hence either θ≤α\theta\le\alpha or θ≥β\theta\ge\beta throughout this connected base interval. After shrinking it, take

yℓ=2α,yh=β/2,α<yℓ<yh<β. y_\ell=2\alpha,\qquad y_h=\beta/2, \qquad \alpha<y_\ell<y_h<\beta.

The actual ratio is

f(x,yh)f(x,yℓ)=4α(x)β(x)⟶0. \frac{f(x,y_h)}{f(x,y_\ell)} =\frac{4\alpha(x)}{\beta(x)}\longrightarrow0.

If θ≤α\theta\le\alpha, the distance ratio is at least one, so the prepared ratio is at least m/Mm/M. If θ≥β\theta\ge\beta, then

θ−yhθ−yℓ≥12, \frac{\theta-y_h}{\theta-y_\ell}\ge\frac12,

so the prepared ratio is at least 2−rm/M2^{-r}m/M. Both contradict its limit zero. Some negative exponent is therefore necessary. Boundedness of the whole function does not force nondegenerate preparation; its base coefficient can compensate for an inverse power on a narrowing band.

16. Even substitutions and parameter-dependent poles

Level: intermediate. Explain why the substitution t=τ2t=\tau^2 does not make t\sqrt t analytic on a two-sided neighborhood of zero, while t=τ4t=\tau^4 does. Then analyze the globally subanalytic function

f(x,t)=xt−1/2+t1/3,x∈ℝ,0<t<1. f(x,t)=xt^{-1/2}+t^{1/3}, \qquad x\in\mathbb R,\quad 0<t<1.

Give one common root-variable Laurent expansion and one even substitution that agrees with the actual function for both signs of the new variable. Determine the parameter pieces on which a continuous analytic extension at zero is possible.

Solution. The two compositions are |τ||\tau| and τ2\tau^2. A two-sided analytic substitution must make every cleared exponent even, not merely make the substitution exponent even.

With t=τ6t=\tau^6 on the positive τ\tau-axis the Laurent expansion is

f(x,τ6)=xτ−3+τ2,τ>0. f(x,\tau^6)=x\tau^{-3}+\tau^2,\qquad \tau>0.

For both signs, choose t=τ12t=\tau^{12}. Then

f(x,τ12)=xτ−6+τ4,τ≠0. f(x,\tau^{12})=x\tau^{-6}+\tau^4,\qquad \tau\ne0.

For x≠0x\ne0 the pole remains; no continuous extension is possible there. On the parameter cell {0}\{0\}, the function becomes τ4\tau^4, analytic across zero. The cells (−∞,0),{0},(0,∞)(-\infty,0),\{0\},(0,\infty) give one finite analytic parameter partition.

Even at (x,t)=(0,0)(x,t)=(0,0), continuity fails if one keeps all parameters together. Along x=t1/4x=t^{1/4}, the first summand equals t−1/4t^{-1/4} and diverges. The continuous-parameter theorem requires joint continuity on its stated neighborhood; continuity on the one slice x=0x=0 does not supply that hypothesis.

Compatible triangulations on arbitrary analytic manifolds

Manifold triangulation theorem. Let M be a Hausdorff second-countable real analytic manifold without boundary, of finite dimension, and let its subanalytic subsets form a locally finite family. There is a countable locally finite linear simplicial complex with closed support in a finite Euclidean space and a subanalytic homeomorphism from that support to M, compatible with the family. On every open simplex the map is an analytic diffeomorphism onto an analytic embedded submanifold.

We prove the globalization from the relative polyhedron theorem above. The proof includes the finite-colour covering lemma, finite-regularity subanalytic cutoffs, a proper embedding, bounded proper-image calculus, the extraction of a closed subcomplex and analytic chart-coordinate recovery. The relative theorem’s expressly stated lower prerequisites remain in force. They are separate from the elementary covering and cutoff arguments proved here.

Finite-regularity subanalytic cutoffs on arbitrary analytic manifolds

This is a bounded teaching proof for the cutoff and partition-of-unity dependency in the SH-03 manifold embedding construction. It treats Hausdorff, second-countable, finite-dimensional real analytic manifolds. Fix a finite integer r≥1r\geq1. Every function constructed below is CrC^r, and its graph is locally semianalytic, hence locally subanalytic, in the indicated analytic manifold. The word “subanalytic” here concerns every ambient point of that graph; it does not assert a single globally definable Euclidean presentation at infinity.

Related cutoff constructions are treated in Marja Kankaanrinta, A subanalytic triangulation theorem for real analytic orbifolds, arXiv:1105.0209v2, §5. Its closed-set separation lemma cites Proposition 5.4 of Kankaanrinta’s 1991 dissertation. The proof below supplies the manifold separation and support construction directly, without taking that unread proposition as a prerequisite. It also supplies the finite CrC^r regularity needed for the embedding’s differential-rank argument. Kankaanrinta’s §5 is the comparison source for the construction, not the source of this stronger stated regularity.

Statements and support convention

For a function ff on MM, write

supp⁡Mf={x∈M:f(x)≠0}¯M. \operatorname{supp}_M f=\overline{\{x\in M:f(x)\ne0\}}^{\,M}.

The following statements will be proved.

  1. Every open cover 𝒰\mathcal U of MM, with no subanalyticity hypothesis on its members, admits a countable CrC^r, locally subanalytic partition of unity (λi)(\lambda_i). Each support is compact, lies in one analytic chart and in one member of 𝒰\mathcal U, and the support family is locally finite in MM.
  2. For arbitrary disjoint closed subsets A,B⊂MA,B\subset M, there is a CrC^r, locally subanalytic f:M→[0,1]f:M\to[0,1] with f|A=0f|_A=0 and f|B=1f|_B=1.
  3. If A⊂MA\subset M is closed and A⊂WA\subset W, where WW is open, there is a CrC^r, locally subanalytic h:M→[0,1]h:M\to[0,1] with h|A=1h|_A=1 and supp⁡Mh⊂W\operatorname{supp}_M h\subset W. If AA is compact, hh can have compact support in WW; if WW lies in an analytic chart, that compact support lies in that chart.

Compactness in statement 3 requires a compact inner set. If AA is noncompact, a compactly supported function equal to one on AA is impossible. The general statement instead supplies a support contained in a locally finite union of compact coordinate-ball supports. All partition members in statement 1 individually have compact supports.

The empty manifold and an empty inner set have the empty partition and zero cutoff, respectively. All remaining arguments assume the relevant set is nonempty.

1. The compact radial bump, including derivative checks

Choose rational data c∈ℚnc\in\mathbb Q^n and 0<ρ<R0<\rho<R in ℚ\mathbb Q. Set a=ρ2a=\rho^2, b=R2b=R^2, p=r+1p=r+1, and t+=max⁡(t,0)t_+=\max(t,0). For a real variable qq, define

u(q)=(b−q)+p,v(q)=(q−a)+p,θ(q)=u(q)u(q)+v(q).(C1) u(q)=(b-q)_+^p,\qquad v(q)=(q-a)_+^p, \qquad\theta(q)=\frac{u(q)}{u(q)+v(q)}. \qquad\text{(C1)}

The denominator is strictly positive for every real qq: if q≤aq\leq a, then b−q>0b-q>0; if q≥bq\geq b, then q−a>0q-a>0; and between aa and bb both are positive. Thus

θ(q)={1,q≤a,(b−q)p(b−q)p+(q−a)p,a≤q≤b,0,q≥b.(C2) \theta(q)= \begin{cases} 1,&q\leq a,\\ \displaystyle\frac{(b-q)^p}{(b-q)^p+(q-a)^p},&a\leq q\leq b,\\ 0,&q\geq b. \end{cases} \qquad\text{(C2)}

The graph of this function is semialgebraic: on the three polynomial-inequality regions it is specified by t=1t=1, tD=(b−q)ptD=(b-q)^p with D=(b−q)p+(q−a)p>0D=(b-q)^p+(q-a)^p>0, and t=0t=0, respectively. Overlapping endpoints give the same value. Non-strict inequalities are expressible using strict inequalities and equalities. Consequently, no projection theorem or o-minimal result is needed for this graph description.

The function t↦t+pt\mapsto t_+^p is Cp−1=CrC^{p-1}=C^r. Indeed, its derivatives through order p−1p-1 on the positive half-line are constant multiples of tp−kt^{p-k}, which tend to zero at the origin, matching the zero derivatives on the negative half-line. Its quotient in (C1) is therefore CrC^r. Equivalently, near aa from above,

1−θ(q)=(q−a)pD(q), 1-\theta(q)=\frac{(q-a)^p}{D(q)},

and near bb from below,

θ(q)=(b−q)pD(q). \theta(q)=\frac{(b-q)^p}{D(q)}.

Since D(a)=D(b)=(b−a)p>0D(a)=D(b)=(b-a)^p>0, these expressions have zero derivatives of all orders 1,…,r1,\ldots,r at their joining endpoints. In particular, for the required C1C^1 case p=2p=2, and more generally for p≥2p\geq2,

θ′(q)=−p(b−a)(b−q)p−1(q−a)p−1((b−q)p+(q−a)p)2(a<q<b),(C3) \theta'(q)= -\frac{p(b-a)(b-q)^{p-1}(q-a)^{p-1}}{\big((b-q)^p+(q-a)^p\big)^2} \quad(a<q<b), \qquad\text{(C3)}

and θ′=0\theta'=0 outside this interval and at both endpoints. The displayed derivative tends to zero there.

Let ϕ:V→Ω⊂ℝn\phi:V\to\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be an analytic chart such that B(c,R)¯⊂Ω\overline{B(c,R)}\subset\Omega. Define

β(x)={θ(|ϕ(x)−c|2),x∈V,0,x∉V.(C4) \beta(x)= \begin{cases} \theta\bigl(|\phi(x)-c|^2\bigr),&x\in V,\\ 0,&x\notin V. \end{cases} \qquad\text{(C4)}

On VV, composition with the analytic squared norm makes β\beta a CrC^r function, equal to one on the closed inner ball and strictly positive exactly on the open outer ball. In chart coordinates its gradient is

∇z(θ(|z−c|2))=2(z−c)θ′(|z−c|2), \nabla_z\bigl(\theta(|z-c|^2)\bigr)=2(z-c)\theta'(|z-c|^2),

which tends to zero at both joining spheres. Its support in MM is exactly

K=ϕ−1(B(c,R)¯).(C5) K=\phi^{-1}(\overline{B(c,R)}). \qquad\text{(C5)}

This is compact and therefore closed in the Hausdorff manifold MM, and it lies in VV. Every point of M\KM\setminus K, including every point outside VV, has an open neighborhood disjoint from KK; on that neighborhood β=0\beta=0. Thus zero extension introduces neither a continuity nor a differentiability defect at the chart boundary.

The graph is locally semianalytic on VV, by the three analytic branch conditions from (C2) with q=|ϕ(x)−c|2q=|\phi(x)-c|^2; at every point outside KK, the graph is locally the analytic zero graph. These cases cover all ambient graph points, so β:M→ℝ\beta:M\to\mathbb R is locally semianalytic and locally subanalytic globally on MM. A different analytic chart does not change this conclusion: analytic coordinate transitions substitute analytic functions in the finitely many local equations and inequalities. The construction also works for a zero-dimensional chart, where the coordinate ball is the singleton ℝ0\mathbb R^0.

2. A countable locally finite nested coordinate-ball refinement

We prove the topological refinement needed above instead of assuming an analytic partition of unity or requiring a cover member to be subanalytic.

First, there is a countable cover (Ej)j≥1(E_j)_{j\geq1} by open coordinate balls with compact closures in MM. For every point, take a coordinate ball whose closed coordinate ball lies in a chart image; its closure in MM is compact. Second countability gives a countable subcover: for each basis element contained in some member of this cover, select one such member. The selected members cover because a point and a covering neighborhood contain an appropriate basis element. This argument also proves the particular Lindelöf assertion being used.

Construct compact sets KnK_n, n≥1n\geq1, with

Kn−1⊂int⁡Kn,E¯1∪⋯∪E¯n⊂int⁡Kn,M=⋃n≥1int⁡Kn,(C6) K_{n-1}\subset\operatorname{int}K_n, \qquad \overline E_1\cup\cdots\cup\overline E_n\subset\operatorname{int}K_n, \qquad M=\bigcup_{n\geq1}\operatorname{int}K_n, \qquad\text{(C6)}

where K0=K−1=⌀K_0=K_{-1}=\varnothing. At stage nn, cover the compact set Kn−1∪E¯1∪⋯∪E¯nK_{n-1}\cup\overline E_1\cup\cdots\cup\overline E_n by finitely many precompact open coordinate balls, and let KnK_n be the union of their compact closures. The original open balls are an open subset of this union containing the target compact set, which proves its inclusion in int⁡Kn\operatorname{int}K_n. The resulting KnK_n need not be subanalytic. They are only used to organize the choices.

Given any open cover 𝒰\mathcal U, put

Sn=Kn\int⁡Kn−1,Hn=int⁡Kn+1\Kn−2.(C7) S_n=K_n\setminus\operatorname{int}K_{n-1}, \qquad H_n=\operatorname{int}K_{n+1}\setminus K_{n-2}. \qquad\text{(C7)}

The sets SnS_n are compact and cover MM: for any xx, its first membership in some KnK_n places it in SnS_n. Also Sn⊂HnS_n\subset H_n, since Kn⊂int⁡Kn+1K_n\subset\operatorname{int}K_{n+1} and Kn−2⊂int⁡Kn−1K_{n-2}\subset\operatorname{int}K_{n-1}.

At x∈Snx\in S_n, choose Un,x∈𝒰U_{n,x}\in\mathcal U containing xx and an analytic chart around xx. The intersection of this chart, Un,xU_{n,x}, and HnH_n is open. In its chart coordinates, choose a rational center cc and rational 0<ρ<R0<\rho<R such that the inner ball contains the coordinate of xx and the closed outer ball lies in that intersection. To justify the rational choice, first take a small Euclidean neighborhood contained in the target open set, then take c∈ℚnc\in\mathbb Q^n close enough to the coordinate of xx, and choose rational radii satisfying

|ϕ(x)−c|<ρ<R |\phi(x)-c|<\rho<R

with RR smaller than the remaining distance to the boundary of the chosen Euclidean neighborhood. Density of the rationals provides such data.

By compactness, finitely many resulting inner balls cover SnS_n. Write them as Pn,jP_{n,j} and their corresponding compact outer balls as Ln,jL_{n,j}, 1≤j≤mn1\leq j\leq m_n. We have

Pn,j¯⊂int⁡Ln,j,Ln,j⊂Un,j∩Hn,(C8) \overline{P_{n,j}}\subset\operatorname{int}L_{n,j}, \qquad L_{n,j}\subset U_{n,j}\cap H_n, \qquad\text{(C8)}

and every Ln,jL_{n,j} lies compactly inside an analytic chart. The family of all Ln,jL_{n,j} is locally finite in MM. Indeed, if x∈int⁡KNx\in\operatorname{int}K_N, this open neighborhood is disjoint from Ln,jL_{n,j} for every n≥N+2n\geq N+2, because those balls avoid Kn−2⊃KNK_{n-2}\supset K_N. Only finitely many earlier levels remain, with finitely many balls at each level. The inner balls cover MM, and the family is countable.

This proves precisely the needed refinement by nested balls with locally finite compact outer closures. It uses only second countability, the Hausdorff condition, elementary coordinate topology, and finite subcovers of compact sets.

3. Local graph calculus, with the boundedness hypotheses made explicit

For the particular radial bumps and their combinations, even the full general subanalytic image calculus can be avoided. Near any point, only finitely many compact supports from (C8) meet a neighborhood. A member whose support misses the point is identically zero after a further shrinking. For every other member the point lies in its analytic chart. Intersecting these finitely many neighborhoods gives a neighborhood on which each bump has finitely many semianalytic branches with an analytic expression. On a middle branch that expression is rational in analytic functions and its denominator is positive on the branch, as in (C2). Refine by the finitely many simultaneous branch choices. Each resulting piece is semianalytic, and sums, products, and quotients with a positive denominator have analytic expressions on a neighborhood of that piece. Their graphs are specified by analytic equations, or by the same equations after clearing positive denominators. Finite union gives a locally semianalytic graph. This observation will cover all the cutoffs, separation functions, and partitions constructed below.

Here are the corresponding general local subanalytic graph statements useful for other parts of the embedding argument. In these statements functions are continuous; this ensures bounded auxiliary graph coordinates near a fixed point.

G1 — finite tuples. If continuous fj:M→ℝf_j:M\to\mathbb R have locally subanalytic graphs, then the graph of (f1,…,fk)(f_1,\ldots,f_k) is locally subanalytic. In local coordinates, it is the intersection of the analytic inverse images of Γfj\Gamma_{f_j} under (x,t1,…,tk)↦(x,tj)(x,t_1,\ldots,t_k)\mapsto(x,t_j). This uses finite intersection and analytic inverse-image closure.

G2 — sums and products. If f,gf,g are continuous with locally subanalytic graphs, then f+gf+g and fgfg have locally subanalytic graphs. Fix x0x_0, take a relatively compact coordinate neighborhood VV, and shrink it so f,gf,g are bounded on a neighborhood of V¯\overline V. Take bounded open auxiliary intervals containing their ranges there. Intersect the two graph conditions and the analytic equation t=u+vt=u+v, respectively t=uvt=uv, inside these bounded coordinates, also bounding tt. This subanalytic set has compact closure in a larger chart-and-interval neighborhood. Projection to (x,t)(x,t) is analytic and proper on that compact closure, so its image is subanalytic near x0x_0. The projection describes exactly the desired graph. The properness on the closure, not just on the graph set, is the relevant image hypothesis.

G3 — reciprocal and division. If ss is continuous, locally subanalytic, and nonzero everywhere, the graph of 1/s1/s is the analytic inverse image of Γs\Gamma_s under (x,t)↦(x,1/t)(x,t)\mapsto(x,1/t), on the open manifold t≠0t\ne0. At an ambient point with t=0t=0, continuity of ss makes ss bounded near its base point, so reciprocals cannot approach zero there; the graph is locally empty. Alternatively, near x0x_0, |s||s| is bounded above and bounded away from zero, and the bounded graph projection argument applies. Together with G2 this proves the division statement. A positive continuous denominator admits these local bounds even if its global infimum is zero.

G4 — analytic compositions. A continuous locally subanalytic map composed with an analytic map defined on a neighborhood of its local image remains locally subanalytic. Use G1 and the graph equation t=F(u)t=F(u), restricting uu to a compact neighborhood of the image and tt to bounded coordinates, and project as in G2. Analytic chart changes and products with analytic chart coordinates are special cases. For the constructed piecewise analytic functions these cases also follow directly from their finite branch equations.

G5 — locally finite sums. If (fi)(f_i) is a family of CrC^r locally subanalytic functions with locally finite supports in the ambient manifold, then ∑ifi\sum_i f_i is CrC^r and locally subanalytic. Around every point, all but finitely many functions vanish on one neighborhood, so this is a finite sum there. The assertion concerns supports, not merely a pointwise finite count of nonzero values. Derivatives through order rr are those of the finite local sum.

G6 — controlled zero extension. Let V⊂MV\subset M be open and let g:V→ℝkg:V\to\mathbb R^k be CrC^r and locally subanalytic. If

K={x∈V:g(x)≠0}¯M⊂V,(C9) K=\overline{\{x\in V:g(x)\ne0\}}^{\,M}\subset V, \qquad\text{(C9)}

then extending gg by zero to MM preserves both properties. On VV there is no change; each point outside VV lies in the open set M\KM\setminus K, where the extension is identically zero. Compact containment is a sufficient instance of (C9), not a replacement for local subanalyticity of the original graph. In particular, if hh has compact support in an analytic chart ϕ:V→ℝn\phi:V\to\mathbb R^n, the zero extension of hϕh\phi is CrC^r and locally subanalytic by G2/G4/G6. Chart coordinates may be unbounded towards the chart boundary, but every point of that boundary has a neighborhood where this product is zero.

The general facts G1–G4 use the exact lower-calculus prerequisites “finite intersection,” “analytic inverse images,” and “analytic images proper on the closure,” used here with their precise conditions: finite intersections and analytic inverse images preserve local subanalyticity; an analytic image is locally subanalytic when its restriction to the closure of the source set is proper. G5 and G6 are proved here from locality. Their globally subanalytic Euclidean analogues are actually read in Guillaume Valette, On subanalytic geometry, arXiv:2507.23622v1, native analytic_geometry.tex, lines 61–127 (graph definition and Basic Properties). Those global analogues are not applied to an arbitrary open cover or to the whole manifold. The direct finite-branch argument at the start of this section makes the present partition and cutoff conclusions independent of these deeper general closure theorems; they need only the elementary inclusion of semianalytic sets among subanalytic sets.

4. Partition of unity subordinate to an arbitrary open cover

Apply Section 2 to 𝒰\mathcal U, and index the chosen pairs of nested balls by ii. Let βi\beta_i be the CrC^r bump from Section 1, equal to one on the corresponding inner ball and supported on its compact outer ball LiL_i. Define

S(x)=∑iβi(x),λi(x)=βi(x)S(x).(C10) S(x)=\sum_i\beta_i(x), \qquad \lambda_i(x)=\frac{\beta_i(x)}{S(x)}. \qquad\text{(C10)}

The sums are locally finite in a neighborhood, so SS is CrC^r and locally semianalytic by Section 3. Some inner ball contains every xx, and its bump equals one there, hence S(x)≥1S(x)\geq1. Division preserves CrC^r regularity, and the finite branch descriptions prove each quotient locally semianalytic. Alternatively, G3 proves local subanalyticity directly. Thus

0≤λi≤1,∑iλi=1,supp⁡Mλi=supp⁡Mβi=Li⊂Ui∈𝒰.(C11) 0\leq\lambda_i\leq1,\qquad\sum_i\lambda_i=1, \qquad\operatorname{supp}_M\lambda_i =\operatorname{supp}_M\beta_i=L_i\subset U_i\in\mathcal U. \qquad\text{(C11)}

The support equality holds because SS is strictly positive: λi≠0\lambda_i\ne0 exactly where βi≠0\beta_i\ne0. These supports are compact, contained in analytic charts, and locally finite. They cover MM since at every point some λi\lambda_i is positive. This proves statement 1, including all support and smoothness conditions.

If a partition indexed by the original cover members is wanted, choose the recorded assignment i↦α(i)i\mapsto\alpha(i) and put

μα=∑α(i)=αλi. \mu_\alpha=\sum_{\alpha(i)=\alpha}\lambda_i.

It is CrC^r and locally subanalytic; only countably many members are nonzero. Its support is contained in UαU_\alpha and the grouped support family is locally finite. To check this last support assertion rather than assume it, a locally finite union of closed sets is closed: near a point outside the union, first discard all but finitely many sets using local finiteness and then avoid those finitely many closed sets. Therefore the union of LiL_i with α(i)=α\alpha(i)=\alpha is a closed subset of UαU_\alpha containing supp⁡μα\operatorname{supp}\mu_\alpha. A neighborhood meeting only finitely many LiL_i can meet only the finitely many grouped supports with their labels. Grouping can lose compact support in one chart, so the refined partition (C10) is the version used when those conditions matter.

5. Arbitrary closed-set separation without realizing an arbitrary zero set

For disjoint closed A,B⊂MA,B\subset M, the two open sets

M\A,M\B M\setminus A,\qquad M\setminus B

cover MM. Apply the refined partition of Section 4, with each support assigned to one of these two sets. Write IAI_A for indices assigned to M\AM\setminus A, and put

f=∑i∈IAλi.(C12) f=\sum_{i\in I_A}\lambda_i. \qquad\text{(C12)}

This is a locally finite sum, is CrC^r and locally subanalytic, and lies in [0,1][0,1]. At a point of AA, every term in this sum vanishes, since its support is disjoint from AA; hence f|A=0f|_A=0. At a point of BB, every partition term assigned to M\BM\setminus B vanishes, so the remaining terms sum to one; hence f|B=1f|_B=1. This proves statement 2.

In particular, we never cover all of M\AM\setminus A by a support family that is locally finite in MM and demand positivity at every point there. Such a construction would force f−1(0)=Af^{-1}(0)=A, an unjustified condition for an arbitrary closed set. In (C12) the zero set merely contains AA and the one set contains BB. The arbitrary sets are inputs to open-neighborhood choices, not analytic graph constraints.

6. Cutoff plateaus and the nested-shrink use

Let A⊂WA\subset W with AA closed and WW open. Apply Section 4 to the open cover {W,M\A}\{W,M\setminus A\}. If IWI_W consists of indices assigned to WW, set

h=∑i∈IWλi.(C13) h=\sum_{i\in I_W}\lambda_i. \qquad\text{(C13)}

Exactly as in Section 5, 0≤h≤10\leq h\leq1, hh is CrC^r and locally subanalytic, and h|A=1h|_A=1. The closed, locally finite union ⋃i∈IWLi\bigcup_{i\in I_W}L_i lies in WW, so

supp⁡Mh⊂⋃i∈IWLi⊂W.(C14) \operatorname{supp}_M h\subset\bigcup_{i\in I_W}L_i\subset W. \qquad\text{(C14)}

This proves the general cutoff assertion. Notice that zero values on M\WM\setminus W, by themselves, would not establish (C14); the locally finite closed union is the support control.

There is a shorter compact construction that also gives a plateau on an open neighborhood of AA. If AA is compact, choose finitely many nested coordinate balls with outer compact balls contained in WW and with inner open balls covering AA. Let their bumps be β1,…,βm\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m, and set

h=1−∏j=1m(1−βj).(C15) h=1-\prod_{j=1}^m(1-\beta_j). \qquad\text{(C15)}

Each factor lies in [0,1][0,1], so h∈[0,1]h\in[0,1]. On every inner ball some βj=1\beta_j=1, hence h=1h=1. Outside the finite union of outer compact balls all βj=0\beta_j=0, hence h=0h=0. The finite union is a compact subset of WW. Finite products preserve CrC^r regularity and the local finite branch graph description. Thus (C15) is a compactly supported CrC^r, locally subanalytic cutoff equal to one on an open neighborhood of AA. When WW lies in one analytic chart, all the balls can be selected in that chart, so the support lies compactly inside it. One can also form the product locally for a locally finite ball family, but the partition proof (C13) already supplies the general noncompact statement.

For the intended nested-shrink application, assume

V¯M⊂W⊂U,U an analytic chart,V¯M compact.(C16) \overline V^{\,M}\subset W\subset U, \quad U\text{ an analytic chart}, \quad \overline V^{\,M}\text{ compact}. \qquad\text{(C16)}

Formula (C15), applied to A=V¯MA=\overline V^{\,M}, gives

h=1 on V¯M,supp⁡Mh⋐W⊂U,0≤h≤1,(C17) h=1\text{ on }\overline V^{\,M}, \qquad\operatorname{supp}_M h\Subset W\subset U, \qquad0\leq h\leq1, \qquad\text{(C17)}

with CrC^r regularity and a locally semianalytic graph. Here K⋐WK\Subset W means that KK is compact and contained in WW; WW need not be subanalytic. If a locally finite family (Wi)(W_i) and compact inner sets Ai⊂WiA_i\subset W_i are supplied, construct hih_i independently this way. The supports remain locally finite because they are contained in WiW_i. If the inner sets cover MM, then ∑ihi≥1\sum_i h_i\geq1, and (C10) with hih_i in place of βi\beta_i gives the desired partition. This applies to a finite-color family just as to an uncolored locally finite family; no coloring hypothesis enters the cutoff proof.

Finally, for each chart ϕi:Ui→ℝn\phi_i:U_i\to\mathbb R^n, the vector map

x⟼{hi(x)ϕi(x),x∈Ui,0,x∉Ui(C18) x\longmapsto \begin{cases} h_i(x)\phi_i(x),&x\in U_i,\\ 0,&x\notin U_i \end{cases} \qquad\text{(C18)}

is CrC^r and locally subanalytic by the finite branch equations or G2/G4/G6. On the plateau neighborhood it equals ϕi\phi_i, with exactly the chart’s derivatives. This is the cutoff fact needed for the later C1C^1 embedding and coordinate-recovery argument; the embedding itself is outside this bounded proof.

7. Optional finite-group chart statement

Suppose a finite group GG acts analytically on MM, and A,BA,B are invariant disjoint closed sets. Apply Section 5, then average:

f¯(x)=1|G|∑g∈Gf(gx). \overline f(x)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}f(gx).

This function is invariant, CrC^r, locally subanalytic, still in [0,1][0,1], and has the same prescribed zero and one values. Analytic diffeomorphisms preserve the local finite branch equations; the finite sum preserves all regularity. Likewise, if A⊂WA\subset W are invariant and a compact cutoff hh is available, the average is one on AA and has support contained in the finite compact union ⋃g∈Gg−1(supp⁡h)⊂W\bigcup_{g\in G}g^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}h)\subset W. This supplies a bounded finite-group lift of the separation/cutoff fact. No full orbifold atlas-gluing or global quotient theorem is claimed here.

Exact dependency boundary

For the constructed CrC^r partitions and cutoffs, the dependencies are finite-dimensional analytic chart topology; second countability and Hausdorff compactness; density of rational coordinate data; finite subcovers of compact sets; elementary differentiation and division by a nonvanishing CrC^r function; the definition of locally semianalytic sets and its invariance under analytic coordinate changes; and semianalytic inclusion in the local subanalytic class. The compact-exhaustion and locally finite refinement steps are fully proved in Section 2. No analytic partition of unity, analytic embedding theorem, arbitrary globally definable cover, or prescribed subanalyticity of an arbitrary open/closed input set is assumed. General local graph consequences G1–G4 additionally use only the lower calculus stated with its proper-on-closure condition in the owned lesson; those deeper statements are not needed for the explicit finite-branch construction.

Finite-colour refinement for a manifold

This is a complete proof of the manifold case needed by SH-03. It applies to a topological manifold; no differentiable structure is required. The auxiliary nerve need not have a global dimension bound. The construction never triangulates the manifold.

Statement

Let MM be a second-countable Hausdorff topological nn-manifold, n≥0n\geq0, and let 𝒰\mathcal U be any open cover. Then there is a countable locally finite open refinement

𝒪=⋃k=0n𝒪k \mathcal O=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\mathcal O_k

which covers MM, such that distinct members of each 𝒪k\mathcal O_k are disjoint. We can require more: for every O∈𝒪O\in\mathcal O there are an original cover member U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal U and a prescribed-atlas chart domain C⊂MC\subset M such that

O¯ is compact,O¯⊂U∩C.(F1) \overline O\text{ is compact},\qquad \overline O\subset U\cap C. \qquad\text{(F1)}

Thus the statement requested for a second-countable Hausdorff paracompact manifold follows. Paracompactness need not be used separately: the elementary exhaustion below provides the needed locally finite covers. The empty manifold is immediate. The usual convention here is that manifold charts are open subsets of ℝn\mathbb R^n, so no boundary is involved.

Source comparison and provenance

Marja Kankaanrinta, A subanalytic triangulation theorem for real analytic orbifolds, arXiv:1105.0209v2, Section 2, states the finite-colour theorem for a paracompact space of covering dimension nn, attributes the result originally to J. Milnor, and also credits R. S. Palais. Its next paragraph explains the indexing by finite unordered tuples.

John Milnor’s Differential Topology, Princeton lectures, Fall 1958, notes by James Munkres, Lemma 2.19, gives the colouring by strict inequalities between partition coordinates. That text assumes the covering-dimension bound for a manifold. The actual source was read at the opening page (attribution and chapter structure) and printed pages 18–19, especially Lemma 2.19 on printed page 19, PDF page index 18. Available lecture notes.

The strict-inequality colouring in the last section below is this Milnor construction, with its openness and local finiteness checked explicitly. The missing manifold dimension input is supplied here by a proved local approximation lemma and a locally finite elimination of nerve simplices. The resulting proof is an elementary argument. In particular, Palais’s theorem and an asserted equality of manifold and covering dimensions are not dependencies of this proof.

1. Locally finite compact chart supports

We first construct the elementary neighbourhood data used twice in the proof.

A point in an open set A⊂MA\subset M has nested chart cubes W,VW,V such that

x∈W,W¯⊂V,V¯⊂A,V¯ compact.(F2) x\in W,\qquad \overline W\subset V,\qquad \overline V\subset A,\qquad \overline V\text{ compact}. \qquad\text{(F2)}

Indeed, restrict a chart around the point to AA, and choose two nested Euclidean open cubes whose closures lie in its coordinate image. Their closed-cube inverse images are compact and hence closed in the Hausdorff space MM; they are consequently the closures in MM. The chart may be chosen from a supplied atlas and restricted. The same argument works for n=0n=0, when a chart cube is a single isolated point.

There is a countable cover B1,B2,…B_1,B_2,\ldots by such relatively compact chart neighbourhoods. To see the countability, a second-countable space is Lindelöf: from an open cover, select one cover member for each basis element which lies in a cover member. These selected members still cover. Apply this to the cover of all the neighbourhoods just constructed.

There are compact sets KjK_j, j≥0j\geq0, with

K0=⌀,Kj⊂int⁡Kj+1,⋃j≥1int⁡Kj=M.(F3) K_0=\varnothing,\qquad K_j\subset\operatorname{int}K_{j+1},\qquad \bigcup_{j\geq1}\operatorname{int}K_j=M. \qquad\text{(F3)}

Inductively cover the compact set Kj−1∪B¯jK_{j-1}\cup\overline B_j by finitely many relatively compact chart neighbourhoods and let KjK_j be the union of their closures. The open neighbourhoods in that finite cover show that Kj−1∪B¯j⊂int⁡KjK_{j-1}\cup\overline B_j\subset\operatorname{int}K_j. The sets are compact, and every BjB_j is eventually in an interior. Set Kj=⌀K_j=\varnothing for negative jj.

The compact band

Aj=Kj\int⁡Kj−1 A_j=K_j\setminus\operatorname{int}K_{j-1}

lies in the open set

Dj=int⁡Kj+1\Kj−2. D_j=\operatorname{int}K_{j+1}\setminus K_{j-2}.

For every point of AjA_j, use (F2) inside Dj∩U∩CD_j\cap U\cap C, with U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal U containing the point and CC a chosen atlas chart containing it. Select finitely many inner cubes Wj,lW_{j,l} covering AjA_j, and retain their paired outer cubes Vj,lV_{j,l}. Enumerate the pairs as (Wi,Vi)i∈I(W_i,V_i)_{i\in I}, where II is finite or countable. They satisfy

⋃iWi=M,W¯i⊂Vi,V¯i compact in Ui∩Ci.(F4) \bigcup_i W_i=M,\qquad \overline W_i\subset V_i, \qquad \overline V_i\text{ compact in }U_i\cap C_i. \qquad\text{(F4)}

The outer family is locally finite. If x∈int⁡Kmx\in\operatorname{int}K_m, the neighbourhood int⁡Km\operatorname{int}K_m meets none of the cubes belonging to a band j≥m+2j\geq m+2, because these cubes avoid Kj−2⊃KmK_{j-2}\supset K_m. Only finitely many smaller bands exist, and each contributes finitely many cubes. In particular every compact set meets only finitely many ViV_i: use finitely many of these local neighbourhoods to cover the compact set.

Within the coordinates of ViV_i, take a continuous product of one-dimensional hat functions which equals one on W¯i\overline W_i and vanishes outside a smaller closed cube inside ViV_i. Extend it by zero to MM. This gives

0≤bi≤1,bi=1 on W¯i,Qi:=supp⁡bi compact,Qi⊂Vi.(F5) 0\leq b_i\leq1,\qquad b_i=1\text{ on }\overline W_i, \qquad Q_i:=\operatorname{supp}b_i\text{ compact},\quad Q_i\subset V_i. \qquad\text{(F5)}

The zero extension is continuous, since its support is contained in the interior of its chart domain. The family of supports is locally finite. The sum b=∑ibib=\sum_i b_i is therefore continuous and positive, and

fi=bi/b,fi≥0,∑ifi=1(F6) f_i=b_i/b,\qquad f_i\geq0,\qquad \sum_i f_i=1 \qquad\text{(F6)}

is a continuous partition with compact chart supports. All sums are finite on a neighbourhood of each point. This constructs the partition needed here, rather than invoking a partition-of-unity theorem.

Exactly the same construction applies to any open submanifold P⊂MP\subset M, using its own compact exhaustion. It supplies a locally finite family of closed inner cubes covering PP, continuous functions equal to one on those inner cubes, and larger compact chart cubes containing their supports.

2. A proved point-avoidance approximation lemma

Lemma. Suppose PP is a second-countable Hausdorff topological nn-manifold, m>nm>n, u:P→ℝmu:P\to\mathbb R^m is continuous, a∈ℝma\in\mathbb R^m, and ϵ:P→(0,∞)\epsilon:P\to(0,\infty) is continuous. There is a continuous v:P→ℝm\{a}v:P\to\mathbb R^m\setminus\{a\} with

∥v(x)−u(x)∥<ϵ(x)(x∈P).(F7) \|v(x)-u(x)\|<\epsilon(x)\quad(x\in P). \qquad\text{(F7)}

Local approximation. On a closed Euclidean nn-cube LL, every continuous map to ℝm\mathbb R^m can be approximated uniformly within any δ>0\delta>0 by a piecewise affine map missing aa. Subdivide LL into a sufficiently fine finite cubical grid. Each small grid cube is divided into the n!n! simplexes obtained by ordering its nn coordinate increments; these divisions agree on shared faces. Uniform continuity makes the oscillation of uu on each small simplex less than δ/2\delta/2.

Choose the images of the finitely many vertices within δ/2\delta/2 of their original images, as follows. When a new vertex image is chosen, avoid the affine spans of aa together with each collection of at most nn previously chosen vertex images. There are finitely many spans, each of dimension at most n<mn<m. A proper affine subspace is closed with empty interior; a finite union of such subspaces cannot contain a nonempty open ball, by successively choosing a smaller open ball disjoint from each subspace. Thus a permissible new image always exists in the required small ball. The construction ensures that aa together with any at most n+1n+1 chosen vertex images is affinely independent.

Extend the vertex images affinely over each simplex. The extensions agree on faces. No simplex image contains aa, because that would put aa in the affine span of at most n+1n+1 of its vertex images. Barycentric interpolation and the oscillation bound give uniform error less than δ\delta. This is only an explicit finite decomposition of a Euclidean cube, not a triangulation of PP.

Global construction. Use the end of Section 1 on PP to obtain closed inner chart cubes HiH_i covering PP, larger closed chart cubes LiL_i, and continuous functions χi\chi_i such that

0≤χi≤1,χi=1 on Hi,supp⁡χi⊂int⁡Li. 0\leq\chi_i\leq1,\quad \chi_i=1\text{ on }H_i, \quad\operatorname{supp}\chi_i\subset\operatorname{int}L_i.

Choose these so that the family LiL_i is locally finite. Put u0=uu_0=u. Inductively choose δi>0\delta_i>0 satisfying

δi<2−i−1minLiϵ(F8) \delta_i<2^{-i-1}\min_{L_i}\epsilon \qquad\text{(F8)}

and, when i>1i>1,

δi<12minH1∪⋯∪Hi−1∥ui−1−a∥.(F9) \delta_i<\frac12\min_{H_1\cup\cdots\cup H_{i-1}} \|u_{i-1}-a\|. \qquad\text{(F9)}

The second minimum is positive by the preceding stages and compactness. Empty unions impose no condition. Approximate ui−1|Liu_{i-1}|L_i, in its chart coordinates, by a piecewise affine map pip_i missing aa with error less than δi\delta_i, and define

ui=ui−1+χi(pi−ui−1) on Li,ui=ui−1 elsewhere.(F10) u_i=u_{i-1}+\chi_i(p_i-u_{i-1})\text{ on }L_i, \qquad u_i=u_{i-1}\text{ elsewhere}. \qquad\text{(F10)}

The formula is continuous across the boundary of LiL_i, since χi\chi_i vanishes on a neighbourhood of that boundary. On HiH_i, the new map equals pip_i and avoids aa. Condition (F9) preserves avoidance on all earlier HjH_j. Hence uiu_i avoids aa on H1∪⋯∪HiH_1\cup\cdots\cup H_i.

Every point has a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many LiL_i. Thus uiu_i is eventually constant on that neighbourhood, and the pointwise limit vv is continuous. Each point belongs to some HjH_j, and its final value is a finite-stage value after stage jj; it still avoids aa. At a point changed at stage ii, (F8) bounds the change by 2−i−1ϵ(x)2^{-i-1}\epsilon(x). Therefore

∥v(x)−u(x)∥<∑i≥12−i−1ϵ(x)=12ϵ(x)<ϵ(x). \|v(x)-u(x)\|<\sum_{i\geq1}2^{-i-1}\epsilon(x) =\tfrac12\epsilon(x)<\epsilon(x).

This proves the lemma. It uses neither Sard’s theorem, a smooth approximation theorem, the Baire theorem, nor covering dimension.

3. The nerve is locally finite, and the partition map is proper

Let NN be the nerve of the cover (Vi)i∈I(V_i)_{i\in I}: a nonempty finite set of vertices σ⊂I\sigma\subset I is a simplex when ⋂i∈σVi≠⌀\bigcap_{i\in\sigma}V_i\ne\varnothing. Its realization consists of the finitely supported vectors

|N|={(ti):ti≥0,∑iti=1,{i:ti>0} is a simplex of N} |N|=\{(t_i):t_i\geq0,\ \sum_i t_i=1,\ \{i:t_i>0\}\text{ is a simplex of }N\}

in ℓ2(I)\ell^2(I), with the subspace topology. This agrees with the usual simplex topology for this locally finite complex.

In fact each vertex belongs to only finitely many simplexes. The compact set V¯i\overline V_i meets only finitely many cover members; any simplex containing ii has all its vertices among these finitely many neighbours. There are only finitely many such finite vertex subsets. This proves local finiteness of the complex, but does not supply a uniform bound on its simplex dimensions.

Here are the topology details we will use. At t∈|N|t\in|N|, choose an index ii with ti>0t_i>0. The open neighbourhood

{s∈|N|:si>ti/2}(F11) \{s\in|N|:s_i>t_i/2\} \qquad\text{(F11)}

meets only the finitely many simplexes containing ii. It lies in a finite subcomplex; its closure lies in a compact union of finitely many closed simplexes. Thus |N||N| is locally compact and Hausdorff. The same finite-subcomplex description proves agreement of the two topologies. A compact subset of |N||N| lies in a finite subcomplex: cover it by finitely many neighbourhoods (F11), then take the union of their finite subcomplexes.

The functions (F6) define a map

F:M⟶|N|,F(x)=(fi(x)).(F12) F:M\longrightarrow|N|,\qquad F(x)=(f_i(x)). \qquad\text{(F12)}

Its support is a simplex because fi(x)>0f_i(x)>0 implies x∈Vix\in V_i. Continuity follows from the fact that locally only finitely many of the fif_i occur. If a compact set D⊂|N|D\subset|N| lies in a subcomplex with finite vertex set JJ, then

F−1(D)⊂⋃i∈JQi.(F13) F^{-1}(D)\subset\bigcup_{i\in J}Q_i. \qquad\text{(F13)}

The inverse image is closed and the right side is compact, so FF is proper. It is also a closed map: for a closed A⊂MA\subset M and y∉F(A)y\notin F(A), take a compact neighbourhood DD of yy. The set F(A∩F−1(D))F(A\cap F^{-1}(D)) is compact and closed, so its complement in the interior of DD gives a neighbourhood of yy missing F(A)F(A). In particular F(M)F(M) is closed in |N||N|.

The same argument applies to any continuous G:M→|N|G:M\to|N| for which

Gi(x)>0⟹fi(x)>0.(F14) G_i(x)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ f_i(x)>0. \qquad\text{(F14)}

Such a map remains proper and closed. We will maintain this support condition during the compression. Properness is verified here because it is useful to the intended nerve route; point avoidance itself was proved in Section 2 and does not require closedness of the image.

4. Compress into the nn-skeleton without enlarging supports

We explain one simplex removal first. Let L⊂NL\subset N be a subcomplex, let σ\sigma be a maximal simplex of LL with dimension m>nm>n, and let u:M→|L|u:M\to|L| be continuous. Choose a∈int⁡σa\in\operatorname{int}\sigma, for example its barycentre, and put

P=u−1(int⁡σ). P=u^{-1}(\operatorname{int}\sigma).

The interior of this maximal simplex is open in |L||L|. Indeed, near an interior point all its vertex coordinates are positive; any simplex with those coordinates positive must contain σ\sigma, and maximality forces it to equal σ\sigma. Therefore PP is an open nn-manifold. If PP is empty, the simplex may simply be removed.

Otherwise identify the affine span of σ\sigma with ℝm\mathbb R^m. Apply Section 2 on PP to u|Pu|P, the point aa, and the continuous positive tolerance

ϵ(x)=14min⁡{1,dist⁡(u(x),∂σ)}.(F15) \epsilon(x)=\tfrac14\min\{1,\operatorname{dist}(u(x),\partial\sigma)\}. \qquad\text{(F15)}

We obtain v:P→int⁡σ\{a}v:P\to\operatorname{int}\sigma\setminus\{a\}. The image stays in the simplex interior because its displacement is less than the distance to the boundary. Define ũ=v\widetilde u=v on PP and ũ=u\widetilde u=u elsewhere. This extension is continuous: at z∈∂Pz\in\partial P, continuity and closedness of σ\sigma give u(z)∈∂σu(z)\in\partial\sigma; as x∈Px\in P tends to zz, the bound (F15) tends to zero. The modification has not changed any coordinate outside the carrier σ\sigma, nor introduced or removed vertices within its interior. Thus

supp⁡ũ(x)=supp⁡u(x)for x∈P, \operatorname{supp}\widetilde u(x)=\operatorname{supp}u(x) \quad\text{for }x\in P,

and it is unchanged elsewhere. The map ũ\widetilde u now misses aa everywhere.

Radially retract σ\{a}\sigma\setminus\{a\} to its boundary. In the vertex coordinates of σ\sigma, with ai>0a_i>0, write

d(q)=maxi∈σ(1−qi/ai)>0,r(q)=a+q−ad(q).(F16) d(q)=\max_{i\in\sigma}(1-q_i/a_i)>0, \qquad r(q)=a+\frac{q-a}{d(q)}. \qquad\text{(F16)}

The maximum is positive for q≠aq\ne a, because the coordinates of both qq and aa sum to one. Since 0<d(q)≤10<d(q)\leq1, the ray reaches the simplex boundary at this parameter; every coordinate of r(q)r(q) is nonnegative, at least one is zero, and their sum is one. If q∈∂σq\in\partial\sigma, some qi=0q_i=0, so d(q)=1d(q)=1 and r(q)=qr(q)=q. The formula is continuous away from aa.

Extend rr by the identity outside int⁡σ\operatorname{int}\sigma. This is a continuous map on |L|\{a}|L|\setminus\{a\}: the two closed pieces σ\{a}\sigma\setminus\{a\} and |L|\int⁡σ|L|\setminus\operatorname{int}\sigma agree on the boundary. Hence

u′=r∘ũ:M⟶|L\{σ}|(F17) u'=r\circ\widetilde u:M\longrightarrow|L\setminus\{\sigma\}| \qquad\text{(F17)}

is continuous, where removing the maximal simplex means removing its interior while retaining all its proper faces. It satisfies

supp⁡u′(x)⊂supp⁡u(x).(F18) \operatorname{supp}u'(x)\subset\operatorname{supp}u(x). \qquad\text{(F18)}

At a point changed by (F17), its former carrier was exactly σ\sigma; the radial retraction replaces this carrier by a proper face.

We now perform such removals for all simplexes of dimension greater than nn. Their dimensions may be unbounded. An ordinary instruction to start at a highest dimension would consequently be invalid. Instead enumerate these simplexes in an arbitrary fixed countable list, and repeatedly remove the first unremoved simplex in that list whose proper cofaces have all been removed.

This process is well defined and eventually removes every listed simplex. Each simplex has only finitely many cofaces, since any one of its vertices belongs to only finitely many simplexes of NN. Among the unremoved cofaces of any unremoved simplex, a maximal one is available for removal. To see eventual removal, induct on the maximum length of a proper-coface chain above a given simplex. Maximal simplexes are immediately available. Once the finitely many proper cofaces of a simplex have been removed, it is available permanently, and only finitely many entries earlier in the fixed list can precede it. Thus it is removed after finitely many more steps. This induction has finite height for each simplex, even though heights are not globally bounded.

Starting with FF, apply (F17) at these stages. Denote the successive maps by F(s)F^{(s)}. Their supports decrease pointwise. At a given x∈Mx\in M, choose a neighbourhood HH meeting only finitely many QiQ_i, with their indices in a finite set JJ. Throughout the construction every image of a point of HH has its support in JJ, by (F18). A simplex removal can change that map on HH only if all vertices of the removed simplex belong to JJ. There are only finitely many such simplexes, and each is removed once. Consequently the maps F(s)F^{(s)} are eventually constant on HH.

Their pointwise limit

G:M⟶|N(n)|(F19) G:M\longrightarrow|N^{(n)}| \qquad\text{(F19)}

is therefore continuous. Its image lies in the nn-skeleton: the interior of every simplex of larger dimension is removed at a finite stage and is never reintroduced. The support condition (F14) holds. In particular

gi≥0,∑igi=1,#{i:gi(x)>0}≤n+1,gi(x)>0⟹fi(x)>0.(F20) g_i\geq0,\qquad \sum_i g_i=1,\qquad \#\{i:g_i(x)>0\}\leq n+1, \qquad g_i(x)>0\Longrightarrow f_i(x)>0. \qquad\text{(F20)}

The family of coordinate supports is still locally finite, each support lies in QiQ_i, and GG, viewed as a map to |N||N|, is proper and closed by (F13)–(F14). These conclusions are valid despite the original nerve’s unbounded global dimension.

5. Colour by the number of strictly dominant coordinates

For every nonempty finite S⊂IS\subset I with 1≤|S|≤n+11\leq|S|\leq n+1, put

OS={x∈M:mini∈Sgi(x)>max({0}∪{gj(x):j∉S})}.(F21) O_S=\left\{x\in M: \min_{i\in S}g_i(x)>\max\bigl(\{0\}\cup\{g_j(x):j\notin S\}\bigr) \right\}. \qquad\text{(F21)}

Use the colour k=|S|−1k=|S|-1, and discard empty sets. Formula (F21) is the strict coordinate version of the open stars of barycentres indexed by faces; the following direct checks avoid needing a barycentric-subdivision theorem.

Openness. On a neighbourhood where the original supports have indices in a finite set JJ, the maximum on the right is the maximum of zero and finitely many continuous functions with indices in J\SJ\setminus S. The minimum on the left is also continuous. Its strict inequality defines an open set. No infinite-intersection openness assertion is being used.

Covering. At xx, let Sx={i:gi(x)>0}S_x=\{i:g_i(x)>0\}. By (F20), this is a nonempty set of at most n+1n+1 indices. Its minimum is positive and all outside coordinates are zero, so x∈OSxx\in O_{S_x}.

Disjointness within one colour. If S≠TS\ne T and |S|=|T||S|=|T|, choose i∈S\Ti\in S\setminus T and j∈T\Sj\in T\setminus S. Membership in OSO_S would give gi>gjg_i>g_j, while membership in OTO_T would give gj>gig_j>g_i. Thus OS∩OT=⌀O_S\cap O_T=\varnothing.

Refinement and closure control. For every i∈Si\in S, (F21) implies gi>0g_i>0. By (F20) and (F5),

OS⊂{gi>0}⊂{fi>0}⊂Qi,OS¯⊂Qi⊂Vi⊂Ui∩Ci.(F22) O_S\subset\{g_i>0\}\subset\{f_i>0\}\subset Q_i, \qquad \overline{O_S}\subset Q_i\subset V_i\subset U_i\cap C_i. \qquad\text{(F22)}

Since QiQ_i is compact and closed, OS¯\overline{O_S} is compact. This proves (F1). In fact (F22) holds simultaneously for all i∈Si\in S.

Countability and local finiteness. The collection of finite subsets of a countable II is countable. On the neighbourhood HH used above, a set OSO_S can meet HH only if S⊂JS\subset J: every index in SS must have positive coordinate there. There are only finitely many such subsets. Thus the whole cover is locally finite. Its family of closures is locally finite as well, since a closure meeting the open set HH implies the corresponding open set meets HH.

This proves the theorem in its full manifold scope.

Dependency and scope verdict

The complete logical route is: compact chart cubes and exhaustion → explicit continuous compact-support partition → locally finite nerve → proved point avoidance on an open manifold → coface-first simplex elimination → Milnor’s strict-inequality colouring. Every step is proved above. The elementary background used is compactness, the Hausdorff property, second countability, uniform continuity on a compact cube, finite affine geometry and finite maxima/minima. No global manifold triangulation, finite-covering-dimension theorem, smoothing theorem, smooth partition theorem or Sard theorem is an unproved primitive. The only simplex decomposition is the explicitly described finite grid decomposition inside one Euclidean chart cube.

The output even gives a cover of multiplicity at most n+1n+1, so the upper covering-dimension bound follows from the construction when that convention is used. Equality of covering dimension with nn is unnecessary and is not claimed as proved here.

For an analytic manifold, CiC_i may be chosen from its analytic atlas. The sets OSO_S are arbitrary open subsets with compact closures inside those charts. The proof does not assert that OSO_S is subanalytic, connected, a ball, or contractible. Subanalytic cutoff functions or any separate definability requirement must be supplied by their own argument. Distinct same-colour open sets are disjoint; pairwise disjointness of their closures is not asserted. The stronger closure inclusion (F22) is the chart-control input established here.

Proper embedding and transport to the manifold

The relative polyhedron theorem above concerns a closed linear polyhedron in Euclidean space. Here we supply the globalization step for an arbitrary Hausdorff second-countable real analytic manifold MM of dimension nn. The family {Sa}\{S_a\} to be triangulated is locally finite in MM; each SaS_a is locally subanalytic. Neither compactness of MM nor a globally definable atlas is assumed.

The construction follows the finite-colour and proper-normalization mechanism in Marja Kankaanrinta, A subanalytic triangulation theorem for real analytic orbifolds, §§5–6. In the manifold case ordinary analytic chart coordinates replace the invariant maps needed for an orbifold. The finite-colour covering and continuously differentiable cutoff lemmas proved above are the topological and function-theoretic ingredients. The relative polyhedron theorem retains its stated lower subanalytic prerequisites; this globalization argument does not supply uniformization or a resolution algorithm.

A finite-coordinate embedding with locally recoverable charts

Choose a countable locally finite refinement OjβO_{j\beta} of a relatively compact analytic chart cover, where 1≤j≤k=n+11\leq j\leq k=n+1, β\beta is a positive integer, and distinct sets of the same colour are disjoint. The closure of each member stays in its assigned chart. Repeated shrinking of this locally finite cover gives three open covers with the same indices and

Ujβ¯⊂Wjβ,Wjβ¯⊂Yjβ,Yjβ¯⊂Ojβ. \overline{U_{j\beta}}\subset W_{j\beta},\qquad \overline{W_{j\beta}}\subset Y_{j\beta},\qquad \overline{Y_{j\beta}}\subset O_{j\beta}.

Here is the shrinking argument with its support condition. Take the proved compact-support partition subordinate to the cover {Ojβ}\{O_{j\beta}\}, and group its terms by their assigned member. The grouped functions still form a partition. Their supports KjβK_{j\beta} lie in OjβO_{j\beta}: a locally finite union of the assigned compact supports is closed in MM, and contained in that member. Each KjβK_{j\beta} is compact, because it is closed and lies in the compact closure of OjβO_{j\beta}. These supports cover MM. In the assigned chart, the compact image of KjβK_{j\beta} has positive distance from the complement of the open image of OjβO_{j\beta}. Take three successively larger sufficiently small distance neighborhoods, with compact closures, to obtain Ujβ,Wjβ,YjβU_{j\beta},W_{j\beta},Y_{j\beta}. They all contain KjβK_{j\beta}, so each family covers MM. They remain locally finite and preserve same-colour disjointness because they are subsets of the original members. This proves the displayed shrinkings without a separate shrinking theorem.

Empty members can be omitted. Local finiteness implies that the closure of the union for one colour equals the union of its member closures. Write Uj,Wj,Yj,OjU_j,W_j,Y_j,O_j for these unions. By the cutoff lemma there are C1C^1, locally subanalytic functions hj,hj′:M→[0,1]h_j,h'_j:M\to[0,1] such that

hj=1 on Uj¯,supp⁡hj⊂Wj,hj′=1 on Wj¯,supp⁡hj′⊂Yj. h_j=1\text{ on }\overline{U_j},\quad \operatorname{supp}h_j\subset W_j,\qquad h'_j=1\text{ on }\overline{W_j},\quad \operatorname{supp}h'_j\subset Y_j.

Let cjβc_{j\beta} be the analytic coordinate map of the assigned chart, restricted to OjβO_{j\beta}. On the disjoint union OjO_j, define

fj(x)=(cjβ(x),β)∈ℝn+1(x∈Ojβ),bj(x)={hj′(x)fj(x),x∈Oj,0,x∉Oj. f_j(x)=(c_{j\beta}(x),\beta)\in\mathbb R^{n+1} \quad (x\in O_{j\beta}), \qquad b_j(x)= \begin{cases} h'_j(x)f_j(x),&x\in O_j,\\ 0,&x\notin O_j. \end{cases}

Each fjf_j is analytic on its open domain. At a point outside OjO_j, local finiteness and Yjβ¯⊂Ojβ\overline{Y_{j\beta}}\subset O_{j\beta} give a neighborhood meeting none of the relevant supports. Thus zero extension makes bjb_j a C1C^1, locally subanalytic map on all of MM. Although the integer labels and chart coordinates need not be bounded globally, only finitely many labelled chart pieces occur near any point. This is precisely the local assertion required for these operations.

Set q=k(n+2)q=k(n+2), and define

F0=(h1,…,hk,b1,…,bk):M⟶ℝq. F_0=(h_1,\ldots,h_k,b_1,\ldots,b_k):M\longrightarrow\mathbb R^q.

We prove that F0F_0 is a topological embedding. If F0(x)=F0(y)F_0(x)=F_0(y), choose (j,β)(j,\beta) with x∈Ujβx\in U_{j\beta}. Then hj(x)=hj(y)=1h_j(x)=h_j(y)=1, so y∈Wjy\in W_j. Since hj′=1h'_j=1 throughout WjW_j, equality of the last coordinate of bjb_j forces y∈Wjβy\in W_{j\beta}. Equality of its first nn coordinates gives cjβ(x)=cjβ(y)c_{j\beta}(x)=c_{j\beta}(y), hence x=yx=y.

For continuity of the inverse, suppose F0(xm)→F0(x)F_0(x_m)\to F_0(x). Again choose x∈Ujβx\in U_{j\beta}. Eventually hj(xm)>0h_j(x_m)>0, so xm∈Wjx_m\in W_j, where bj(xm)=fj(xm)b_j(x_m)=f_j(x_m).
