The integer coordinate of bj(xm)b_j(x_m) tends to β\beta. It therefore equals β\beta eventually. Now xm∈Wjβx_m\in W_{j\beta}, and convergence of the chart coordinates implies xm→xx_m\to x. Manifolds and Euclidean subspaces are first countable, so this sequential criterion proves continuity of F0−1F_0^{-1}.

The integer coordinate is essential in this proof. Positivity of hjh_j alone locates a point in the union WjW_j, not in one specified WjβW_{j\beta}.

There is also a differential observation we will use later. At every xx some hj(x)>0h_j(x)>0. On a neighborhood of that point in WjβW_{j\beta}, the first nn coordinates of bjb_j are the analytic chart coordinates themselves, since hj′=1h'_j=1. Consequently dF0dF_0 is injective. Thus F0F_0 is a C1C^1 embedding with local analytic coordinates among its blocks, despite not being analytic across all cutoff boundaries.

Properness by one extra coordinate

Choose a countable locally finite C1C^1, locally subanalytic partition of unity {λi}i≥1\{\lambda_i\}_{i\geq1} with compact supports, and put

λ(x)=∑i≥12−iλi(x),F(x)=(F0(x),1)λ(x)∈ℝq+1. \lambda(x)=\sum_{i\geq1}2^{-i}\lambda_i(x),\qquad F(x)=\frac{(F_0(x),1)}{\lambda(x)}\in\mathbb R^{q+1}.

The sum is finite near every point. It follows that λ\lambda is C1C^1, locally subanalytic and strictly positive, with λ≤1/2\lambda\leq1/2. Coordinate ratios recover F0F_0 from FF, so FF remains a C1C^1 topological embedding and an immersion.

For ϵ>0\epsilon>0, choose NN with 2−(N+1)<ϵ2^{-(N+1)}<\epsilon. Outside ⋃i=1Nsupp⁡λi\bigcup_{i=1}^N\operatorname{supp}\lambda_i,

λ(x)=∑i>N2−iλi(x)≤2−(N+1)∑i>Nλi(x)≤2−(N+1)<ϵ. \lambda(x)=\sum_{i>N}2^{-i}\lambda_i(x) \leq 2^{-(N+1)}\sum_{i>N}\lambda_i(x) \leq2^{-(N+1)}<\epsilon.

Thus {λ≥ϵ}\{\lambda\geq\epsilon\} is a closed subset of a finite union of compact supports and is compact. If C⊂ℝq+1C\subset\mathbb R^{q+1} is compact, its last coordinate is bounded above by some R>0R>0. Since the last coordinate of FF is 1/λ1/\lambda, its inverse image is a closed subset of {λ≥1/R}\{\lambda\geq1/R\}. Hence F−1(C)F^{-1}(C) is compact. This proves properness directly, without a second limit-point argument.

A proper map from a locally compact space to Euclidean space is closed here: if F(xm)F(x_m) converges, the sequence lies in a compact Euclidean set, its inverse image is compact, and a convergent subsequence has the required image limit. Therefore Z=F(M)Z=F(M) is closed.

The proper-image calculus needed in this construction

We give the bounded local argument rather than infer global definability from the existence of an atlas. Let P:M→ℝrP:M\to\mathbb R^r be continuous, proper and locally subanalytic, and let A⊂MA\subset M be locally subanalytic. Fix a target point yy and ρ>0\rho>0. The set

K=P−1(B¯(y,2ρ)) K=P^{-1}\bigl(\overline B(y,2\rho)\bigr)

is compact. Cover KK by finitely many closed analytic coordinate boxes QℓQ_\ell, each contained in a chart neighborhood where AA and the graph of PP are locally subanalytic. Choose the boxes small enough that their interiors cover KK. By continuity, P(Qℓ)P(Q_\ell) is bounded. The bounded-chart comparison proved in the analytic preparation component makes

{(u,P(u)):u∈Qℓ∩A} \{(u,P(u)):u\in Q_\ell\cap A\}

a bounded globally subanalytic set in chart and target coordinates. One can see this comparison at every point of its ambient closure: the source coordinate is in QℓQ_\ell, the target coordinate is P(u)P(u) by continuity, and the box lies strictly inside the chart. Thus no witness is being extended past its analytic domain.

Project these finitely many graph traces to the target and intersect with B(y,ρ)B(y,\rho). Their union is exactly P(A)∩B(y,ρ)P(A)\cap B(y,\rho). Indeed any source point mapping into that ball belongs to KK, which the boxes cover. Conversely every projected point comes from AA. The proved finite Boolean and projection calculus therefore makes P(A)P(A) locally subanalytic. This establishes the proper-image assertion in the generality used here, including the C1C^1 map FF.

Properness also carries local finiteness to the target. A compact inverse image of B¯(y,2ρ)\overline B(y,2\rho) has a finite neighborhood cover, each member meeting only finitely many SaS_a. Hence only finitely many F(Sa)F(S_a) meet B(y,ρ)B(y,\rho). This proves ambient local finiteness even at points outside ZZ, rather than just local finiteness in ZZ.

The subanalytic structure does not depend on the chosen proper embedding. If G:M→ℝsG:M\to\mathbb R^s is another continuous proper locally subanalytic topological embedding, then (F,G)(F,G) is proper: the inverse image of a compact product is closed in the compact inverse image under FF of its first projection. Its image is the graph of G∘F−1G\circ F^{-1}, and is locally subanalytic by the argument just given. Swapping the factors gives the graph of the inverse. Thus the comparison is a subanalytic homeomorphism.

A closed ambient polyhedron and the subcomplex it induces

Put d=q+1d=q+1. There is an explicit locally finite linear triangulation KK of all of ℝd\mathbb R^d. For each integer vector mm and each permutation π\pi of {1,…,d}\{1,\ldots,d\}, take the simplex with vertices

m,m+eπ(1),m+eπ(1)+eπ(2),…,m+eπ(1)+⋯+eπ(d). m,\quad m+e_{\pi(1)},\quad m+e_{\pi(1)}+e_{\pi(2)},\quad\ldots,\quad m+e_{\pi(1)}+\cdots+e_{\pi(d)}.

These simplices fill the unit cube m+[0,1]dm+[0,1]^d: order the fractional coordinates of a point, and express it by the successive coordinate differences as nonnegative barycentric weights. On a cube face, the coordinates fixed at zero or one drop out, leaving the same construction in the remaining coordinates. Thus adjacent cubes give the same subdivision of their common face. Include every simplex face. Any compact set meets finitely many unit cubes and finitely many of their simplices, proving local finiteness. Its support is the closed set ℝd\mathbb R^d.

Apply the relative polyhedron theorem to KK, with the locally finite subanalytic family consisting of ZZ and all F(Sa)F(S_a). It gives a subdivision K′K' and a subanalytic homeomorphism T:ℝd→ℝdT:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d, analytic with injective differential on each new open simplex, compatible with the whole family.

Let LL consist of the simplices σ∈K′\sigma\in K' for which T(σ∘)⊂ZT(\sigma^\circ)\subset Z. This is a subcomplex. In fact, closedness of ZZ implies

T(σ)=T(σ∘)¯⊂Z. T(\sigma)=\overline{T(\sigma^\circ)}\subset Z.

Every face of σ\sigma consequently has its open image in ZZ, and belongs to LL. Conversely compatibility says that every point of ZZ lies in the image of an included open simplex. Hence T(|L|)=ZT(|L|)=Z. As a subcomplex, LL is locally finite. It is countable, since each compact integer box meets finitely many simplices and these boxes exhaust the ambient space. Its support |L|=T−1(Z)|L|=T^{-1}(Z) is closed.

The map

t=F−1∘T||L|:|L|⟶M t=F^{-1}\circ T|_{|L|}:|L|\longrightarrow M

is a homeomorphism, compatible with every SaS_a. It and its inverse are locally subanalytic. To verify this without a nonproper-composition assumption, restrict to compact coordinate and simplex boxes. The graph of the composition is obtained by intersecting the two bounded subanalytic graphs along their common ZZ-coordinate and projecting; the middle coordinate is bounded because the maps are continuous on the chosen compact sets. The bounded comparison and projection calculus apply. Such boxes cover neighborhoods of every graph point in both directions.

Why the open simplices are analytic embedded submanifolds

Subanalyticity of tt alone does not imply analyticity on an open simplex. We use the special coordinate blocks in FF.

Let σ∈L\sigma\in L, and write v(u)=T(u)v(u)=T(u) for u∈σ∘u\in\sigma^\circ. The last coordinate vdv_d is positive. Every coordinate of F0(t(u))F_0(t(u)) is the analytic ratio vℓ(u)/vd(u)v_\ell(u)/v_d(u). Given u0u_0, choose (j,β)(j,\beta) with t(u0)∈Ujβt(u_0)\in U_{j\beta}. Near u0u_0 we have hj(t(u))>0h_j(t(u))>0, so t(u)∈Wjt(u)\in W_j and hj′(t(u))=1h'_j(t(u))=1. The corresponding integer coordinate is continuous and integer-valued there, and hence locally equals β\beta. The first nn coordinates of the jj-th block are therefore exactly

cjβ(t(u)). c_{j\beta}(t(u)).

They are the analytic coordinate ratios just identified. The analytic inverse of the chart shows that t|σ∘t|_{\sigma^\circ} is analytic near u0u_0. Since u0u_0 was arbitrary, it is analytic throughout the open simplex.

Its differential is injective. Indeed T|σ∘=F∘t|σ∘T|_{\sigma^\circ}=F\circ t|_{\sigma^\circ}, and FF is C1C^1. The chain rule gives

rank⁡d(T|σ∘)≤rank⁡d(t|σ∘)≤dim⁡σ. \operatorname{rank}d(T|_{\sigma^\circ}) \leq\operatorname{rank}d(t|_{\sigma^\circ}) \leq\dim\sigma.

The left side equals dim⁡σ\dim\sigma by the relative polyhedron theorem. Thus both inequalities are equalities. The analytic constant-rank theorem gives local analytic immersion charts. Since tt is a homeomorphism on the entire support, its restriction is a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology. Consequently the image is an analytic embedded submanifold and the restriction is an analytic diffeomorphism onto it. In particular no simplex has dimension greater than nn.

We have proved the arbitrary-manifold triangulation statement from the displayed lower prerequisites, with no analytic embedding theorem for MM and no global analyticity assertion for the cutoff construction. The C1C^1 regularity was used only in the chain-rule rank argument; finite-colour chart blocks supplied the analyticity of each transported simplex. ▫\square

Exercises on the globalization mechanism

Integer labels identify the chart piece

Suppose W=∐β≥1WβW=\coprod_{\beta\geq1}W_\beta is a disjoint union of open chart pieces and the coordinate map on each piece is cβc_\beta. On WW consider b(x)=(cβ(x),β)b(x)=(c_\beta(x),\beta). If b(xm)→b(x)b(x_m)\to b(x) with x∈Wβx\in W_\beta, prove that xmx_m eventually belongs to WβW_\beta, and explain why merely knowing xm∈Wx_m\in W is insufficient. Give a counterexample to discarding the integer coordinate.

Solution. The last coordinates are positive integers tending to β\beta. Eventually their distance from β\beta is less than 1/21/2, which forces equality. Hence eventually xm∈Wβx_m\in W_\beta. The first coordinates then converge to cβ(x)c_\beta(x); the continuous inverse of the one fixed chart gives xm→xx_m\to x.

For the counterexample let M=∐β≥1(−1,1)βM=\coprod_{\beta\geq1}(-1,1)_\beta, a second-countable real analytic one-manifold, with its usual coordinate on each component. Take x=(0,1)x=(0,1) and xm=(0,m+1)x_m=(0,m+1). The unlabelled coordinate map sends all these points to zero, although the sequence does not converge to xx: the open first component is a neighborhood containing none of its terms. It also fails injectivity. The example concerns the local chart-piece identification step; it is not a proposed compact-support atlas for the global construction. In that construction positivity of hjh_j first places the sequence in WjW_j, and the unscaled integer coordinate then provides the additional localization.

A weighted partition detects escape from every compact set

Let {λi}i≥1\{\lambda_i\}_{i\geq1} be a locally finite partition of unity on MM, with compact supports, and let λ=∑i2−iλi\lambda=\sum_i2^{-i}\lambda_i. Prove that {λ≥ϵ}\{\lambda\geq\epsilon\} is compact for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0. If a sequence xmx_m eventually leaves every compact subset of MM, show that 1/λ(xm)→+∞1/\lambda(x_m)\to+\infty. Explain how this makes (F0,1)/λ(F_0,1)/\lambda proper even when the image of F0F_0 is bounded.

Solution. Choose NN with 2−(N+1)<ϵ2^{-(N+1)}<\epsilon. Outside the finite compact union CN=⋃i≤Nsupp⁡λiC_N=\bigcup_{i\leq N}\operatorname{supp}\lambda_i, the partition identity gives

λ(x)≤2−(N+1)∑i>Nλi(x)≤2−(N+1)<ϵ. \lambda(x)\leq2^{-(N+1)}\sum_{i>N}\lambda_i(x) \leq2^{-(N+1)}<\epsilon.

Consequently {λ≥ϵ}\{\lambda\geq\epsilon\} is a closed subset of CNC_N, and is compact. An escaping sequence eventually avoids this set for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0; hence λ(xm)→0\lambda(x_m)\to0 and its reciprocal tends to infinity.

For a compact target set, bound its last coordinate above by R>0R>0. Its inverse image under (F0,1)/λ(F_0,1)/\lambda is closed and lies in the compact set {λ≥1/R}\{\lambda\geq1/R\}. It is therefore compact. Boundedness of the other coordinates has no effect on this conclusion. The single positive last coordinate carries the entire properness argument.

An analytic homeomorphism can have a zero differential

On (−1,1)(-1,1), let t(u)=u3t(u)=u^3, F(x)=x3F(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}, and T=F∘tT=F\circ t. Check that FF is a proper locally subanalytic topological embedding, that TT is an analytic immersion, and that tt is an analytic homeomorphism whose differential is not injective at zero. Identify the missing hypothesis in an attempted chain-rule rank argument. Contrast this with the C1C^1 map in the globalization proof.

Solution. Regard all three maps as maps from (−1,1)(-1,1) to itself. The cube-root map is a homeomorphism, so the inverse image of a compact set is compact. Its graph is given by y3=xy^3=x, and is semialgebraic, hence locally subanalytic. The composite is T(u)=uT(u)=u, with differential equal to one. The map tt is analytic and bijective with continuous inverse, but t′(0)=0t'(0)=0. Thus an analytic homeomorphism need not be an analytic immersion or an analytic diffeomorphism.

The cube root is not differentiable at zero: h3/h=|h|−2/3\sqrt[3]{h}/h=|h|^{-2/3} for nonzero hh, which diverges. One cannot apply the chain rule there. In the globalization proof the constructed embedding is C1C^1; once chart-coordinate ratios prove that the transported simplex map is analytic, the chain rule is valid. Since TT has rank dim⁡σ\dim\sigma, it forces the transported map to have the same rank. The cutoff’s finite differentiability is therefore a substantive hypothesis in that step.

Closedness and ambient local finiteness do different jobs

Triangulate [0,1][0,1] by its two vertices and one edge. For Z=(0,1)Z=(0,1), collect simplices whose open interiors are contained in ZZ. Explain why this collection is not a subcomplex. Next let F:ℝ→(−1,1)⊂ℝF:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)\subset\mathbb R be F(x)=x/1+x2F(x)=x/\sqrt{1+x^2}, and let Sm={m}S_m=\{m\}, m≥1m\geq1. Verify that {Sm}\{S_m\} is locally finite in ℝ\mathbb R, whereas {F(Sm)}\{F(S_m)\} is not locally finite in the ambient target ℝ\mathbb R. State where properness repairs each problem in the theorem.

Solution. The open edge is (0,1)(0,1), so the edge is selected. Neither endpoint is in ZZ, so neither vertex is selected. A simplicial subcomplex must contain every face of a selected simplex, and this collection fails that condition. When ZZ is closed instead, T(σ∘)⊂ZT(\sigma^\circ)\subset Z implies T(σ)⊂ZT(\sigma)\subset Z, because a continuous homeomorphism takes the closure of the open simplex to the closed simplex image. Every face is then selected as well.

Every bounded interval in the source meets finitely many positive integers; this proves local finiteness of the family {Sm}\{S_m\}. But

F(m)=m1+m2⟶1. F(m)=\frac{m}{\sqrt{1+m^2}}\longrightarrow1.

Every ambient neighborhood of 11 meets infinitely many of these singleton images. The map is not proper as a map to ℝ\mathbb R: the inverse image of the compact set [0,1][0,1] is the noncompact set [0,∞)[0,\infty). Its image is also not closed in that ambient space.

For the theorem’s proper embedding, the image is closed, which makes the selected simplices face-closed. Separately, the compact inverse image of a closed target ball meets only finitely many members of a locally finite source family, which establishes local finiteness in the whole target. Local finiteness only inside the image would not justify the ambient relative polyhedron theorem.

Exercises on compatible analytic partitions

Restriction rank must be calculated again

Exercise P1 (intermediate). Let f(x,y)=xf(x,y)=x, g(x,y)=yg(x,y)=y on ℝ2\mathbb R^2, and prescribe compatibility with the analytic line S={x=0}S=\{x=0\}. Both ambient maps have constant rank one. Give a connected analytic partition compatible with SS, compute both restriction ranks, and explain why decomposing only by ambient rank misses a necessary calculation.

Solution. The three members {x<0}\{x<0\}, SS, and {x>0}\{x>0\} form a finite compatible partition into connected analytic embedded submanifolds. On each open half-plane, the tangent space is ℝ2\mathbb R^2, so both coordinate projections have rank one. On SS, the tangent vectors are (0,v)(0,v). The differential of f|Sf|_S is zero, while that of g|Sg|_S sends (0,v)(0,v) to vv; their ranks are zero and one respectively. An ambient rank decomposition has only the rank-one set for each map, so it gives no information about the rank after a lower-dimensional compatibility refinement. The partition proof recalculates the differentials in each smaller member’s own coordinates.

Accumulation prevents local finiteness

Exercise P2 (introductory). On ℝ\mathbb R, each singleton An={1/n}A_n=\{1/n\}, n≥1n\geq1, is semianalytic. Prove that there is no locally finite partition into connected analytic submanifolds compatible with every AnA_n. Compare with the family {{m}:m∈ℤ}\{\{m\}:m\in\mathbb Z\}, and give an explicit compatible locally finite partition for that family.

Solution. If a partition member contains 1/n1/n, compatibility makes it a subset of AnA_n, so that member must be exactly {1/n}\{1/n\}. Every neighborhood of zero contains infinitely many of these distinct members, contradicting local finiteness. The prescribed family itself is not locally finite at zero; the theorem’s family hypothesis is therefore substantive even though each individual set has a very simple analytic definition. For the integers, take all singletons {m}\{m\} and all intervals (m,m+1)(m,m+1), m∈ℤm\in\mathbb Z. They are connected analytic submanifolds, cover ℝ\mathbb R disjointly, and are compatible with every integer singleton. A bounded neighborhood of any point meets only finitely many of these members. The partition is locally finite and countable, as required.

Dimension and frontier exercises

These exercises use the complete linked dimension, frontier and parameter-continuity provider. Their adaptation credit and CC BY4.0 terms remain at that provider.

Exercise D1 (basic: two boundaries). In ℝ2\mathbb R^2, calculate the frontier and topological boundary of the unit circle S1S^1 and of the open unit disc. Give their dimensions and identify which strict inequality applies.

Solution. The circle is closed with empty interior in ℝ2\mathbb R^2. Therefore fr⁡S1=⌀\operatorname{fr}S^1=\varnothing, of dimension −1-1, and ∂S1=S1\partial S^1=S^1, of dimension one. Its own dimension is one, so strict frontier decrease holds while strict decrease of topological boundary relative to the set fails. The open disc has dimension two; its closure is the closed disc and both its frontier and its topological boundary are the circle, of dimension one. In both examples the topological boundary has dimension less than the ambient dimension two.

Exercise D2 (intermediate: the exceptional parameter). Let A={(t,x):t>0,x=t}⊂ℝ2A=\{(t,x):t>0,\ x=t\}\subset\mathbb R^2. Determine exactly where (A¯)t=At¯(\overline A)_t=\overline{A_t} fails. Give a base partition satisfying (D10), and explain why restricting before taking closure matters.

Solution. For t>0t>0, both sets are {t}\{t\}; for t<0t<0, both are empty. At t=0t=0, A0=⌀A_0=\varnothing but (A¯)0={0}(\overline A)_0=\{0\}, so this is the unique exception. Use the partition (−∞,0),{0},(0,∞)( -\infty,0),\{0\},(0,\infty). On its first two pieces the restricted family is empty, and its closure is empty. On the positive piece the fibre equality holds at each parameter in that piece. Although its closure accumulates at parameter zero, zero is not a parameter of that positive piece. Thus (D10) asserts equality on each piece only after restricting the family; it does not assert that the original ambient closure commutes with all fibres.

Exercise D3 (advanced: continuity and bounded transforms). Define

f(t,x)={txt2+x2,(t,x)≠(0,0),0,(t,x)=(0,0). f(t,x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{tx}{t^2+x^2},&(t,x)\ne(0,0),\\ 0,&(t,x)=(0,0). \end{cases}

Show that every xx-fibre is continuous although ff is not jointly continuous. Find a base partition making it continuous on the corresponding product pieces. Finally show why s/(1+s2)s/(1+s^2) cannot replace the injective transform (D16).

Solution. For t≠0t\ne0 the denominator is everywhere positive, so the fibre is continuous. For t=0t=0 the function is identically zero, including at x=0x=0, so that fibre is continuous too. Along x=t≠0x=t\ne0 its value is 1/21/2, whereas at the origin its value is zero. Thus it is not jointly continuous. The partition (−∞,0),{0},(0,∞)( -\infty,0),\{0\},(0,\infty) works: on either open parameter half-line the same positive-denominator formula is continuous jointly; on the zero piece the function is zero. For the last claim let g(0)=1/2g(0)=1/2 and g(t)=2g(t)=2 when t≠0t\ne0. This definable function is discontinuous at zero, but g/(1+g2)=2/5g/(1+g^2)=2/5 everywhere. Continuity of the bounded composite therefore does not imply continuity of gg. The inverse in (D16) is precisely what prevents this loss of information.
